# [Byte Back](https://www.bytebacklaw.com)

# Texas Attorney General Announces First CUBI Settlement

![](https://www.bytebacklaw.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/631/2019/04/Texas_157051216.jpg)

***Keypoint: The Texas Attorney General reached a $1.4 billion settlement with Meta over its alleged violations of Texas’ biometric privacy law.***

On July 30, 2024, the Texas Attorney General [announced](https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/news/releases/attorney-general-ken-paxton-secures-14-billion-settlement-meta-over-its-unauthorized-capture) that it has reached a $1.4 billion [settlement](https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/sites/default/files/images/press/Final%20State%20of%20Texas%20v%20Meta%20Order%202024.pdf) with Meta over its alleged violations of Texas’ “Capture or Use of Biometric Identifier” Act (CUBI). The Attorney General’s press release represents that the settlement, which arises out of a 2022 complaint, is the first under CUBI. It also represents that the settlement “is the largest privacy settlement an Attorney General has ever obtained.”

In the below article, we provide a brief overview of CUBI and the underlying allegations in the complaint.

**What is CUBI?**

While most companies are aware of the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA), the [Texas Capture or Use of Biometric Identifier Act](https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/Docs/BC/htm/BC.503.htm) (CUBI) has received less attention because it lacks a private right of action like BIPA.

CUBI prohibits a person from capturing a biometric identifier of an individual for a commercial purpose unless the person: “(1) informs the individual before capturing the biometric identifier; and (2) receives the individual’s consent to capture the biometric identifier.” CUBI defines “biometric identifier” to mean “a retina or iris scan, fingerprint, voiceprint, or record of hand or face geometry.” The law does not define “commercial purpose” and does not state that the biometric identifier must be used to identify the individual. The law also does not specify how consent should be obtained (e.g., what type of disclosures need to be made).

In addition, CUBI restricts how a person can use a biometric identifier. Specifically, a biometric identifier captured for a commercial purpose cannot be sold, leased or otherwise disclosed to another person unless the transfer satisfies one of the law’s exceptions. CUBI also contains information security and destruction requirements. For more background on CUBI, please see the Texas Attorney General’s [overview](https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection/file-consumer-complaint/consumer-privacy-rights/biometric-identifier-act#:~:text=Texas%20Capture%20Or%20Use%20Of%20Biometric%20Identifier%20Act&text=With%20certain%20exceptions%2C%20CUBI%20also,full%20text%20of%20the%20Act.).

CUBI is enforceable only by the Texas Attorney General. The Attorney General can seek a civil penalty of up to $25,000 per violation. CUBI was first enacted in 2001 and recodified in 2009. As noted, this is the first settlement under the law.

Finally, it is important to note that the complaint was filed in 2022, which is before the Texas legislature [passed](https://www.bytebacklaw.com/category/texas-2023/) the Texas Data Privacy and Security Act (HB 4) in May 2023.

**What Does the Complaint Allege?**

The Attorney General’s [complaint](https://texasattorneygeneral.gov/sites/default/files/images/child-support/State%20of%20Texas%20v.%20Meta%20Platforms%20Inc..pdf) arises out of Meta’s use of “tag suggestions.” According to the complaint, “Tag Suggestions worked by using Facebook’s proprietary facial-recognition process to capture and analyze the records of facial geometry – of both users and non users – obtained from user-uploaded photos and videos.” “Tag Suggestions would then use the captured records of face geometry to compare faces in the photo or video to the faces of individuals in its database. If the Tag Suggestions recognized and identified one of the faces appearing in the photograph, Facebook would suggest to the user the individual’s name, so that the user could tag the individual.” Facebook also used tags to train its facial-recognition algorithm.

The complaint alleges that Meta violated CUBI by failing to obtain informed consent, disclosing biometric identifiers to third parties, and failing to dispose of the biometric identifiers in a reasonable amount of time. Facebook reportedly ran the tag suggestions program from December 2010 until November 2021, when it ended the program after reaching a $650,000,000 BIPA settlement.

The complaint alleges that Meta violated CUBI as well as the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act.

![Photo of David Stauss [Former Attorney]](https://lexblogplatform.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/631/userphoto/7147-1572288796.jpg)

Formerly with Husch Blackwell, David routinely counseled clients on complying with privacy laws such as the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation, the California Consumer Privacy Act, the Colorado Privacy Act, and other state privacy laws.

# McKool Smith Secures Record-Breaking $1.4 Billion Settlement for State of Texas Against Facebook/Meta in Biometric Privacy Dispute

07.30.2024

[Print PDF](/printpilot-pressrelease-365.pdf?1786481166)

McKool Smith, along with Keller Postman and Attorney General Ken Paxton, secured a massive $1.4 Billion settlement on behalf of the State of Texas against Meta Platforms/Facebook. The record-breaking settlement was announced on July 30, 2024 by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. It is the largest settlement ever obtained from an action brought by a single State.

The case was scheduled to be tried to a jury in June, but the parties agreed to settle the dispute on the eve of trial and asked the court to pause the proceeding to finalize the settlement terms.

The suit alleged that Facebook unlawfully captured the biometric identifiers of Texans for a commercial purpose without their informed consent, disclosed those identifiers to others, and failed to destroy collected identifiers within a reasonable time. Facebook’s activities included capturing biometric information billions of times from photos and videos that millions of Facebook users in Texas uploaded to the social media platform. The suit further alleged that Meta misrepresented whether and how it was using biometric identifiers. Along with the Office of the Attorney General for the State of Texas, McKool Smith and Keller Postman claimed that Facebook has, for over a decade, built an Artificial Intelligence empire while capturing the most intimate data of Texans, thereby putting their well-being, safety, and security at risk.

McKool Smith, along with Keller Postman and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, secured a record-breaking $1.4 billion settlement against Meta Platforms/Facebook on behalf of the State of Texas, announced on July 30, 2024. This is the largest settlement ever obtained from an action brought by a single state. The case (State of Texas v. Meta Platforms, Inc., case no. 22-0121, 71st Judicial District Court for Harrison County, Texas) was scheduled for trial in June 2024 but settled on the eve of trial.

The lawsuit alleged that Facebook unlawfully captured Texans' biometric identifiers billions of times from photos and videos for commercial purposes without informed consent, disclosed those identifiers to others, and failed to destroy them within a reasonable time. It also alleged Meta misrepresented its use of biometric identifiers and built an "Artificial Intelligence empire" using Texans' most intimate data over more than a decade.

Lead counsel Sam Baxter and Jennifer Truelove from McKool Smith led the trial team, which included numerous firm principals and associates. Attorney General Paxton stated the settlement demonstrates Texas' commitment to holding big technology companies accountable for violating citizens' privacy rights.

Meta Settles Texas Biometric Data Lawsuit for Record $1.4 Billion

1 Minute Read

Categories: [Information Security](/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/category/information-security), [Online Privacy](/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/category/online-privacy), [U.S. State Law](/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/category/u-s-state-law)

On July 30, 2024, Texas AG Ken Paxton [announced](https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/news/releases/attorney-general-ken-paxton-secures-14-billion-settlement-meta-over-its-unauthorized-capture) that Meta agreed to pay $1.4 billion to settle a [lawsuit](/privacy-and-information-security-law/texas-ag-sues-meta-over-collection-and-use-of-biometric-data) over allegations that Meta processed facial geometry data of Texas residents in violation of Texas law, including the Texas Capture or Use of Biometric Identifier Act (“CUBI”).

This is the first lawsuit brought and first settlement obtained under CUBI, which was passed in 2009. Filed in 2022, the lawsuit alleged that Meta violated Texas law by, among other things, collecting and analyzing individuals’ facial geometric data (which constitutes biometric data under CUBI) in connection with the “tag suggestions” [feature](/privacy-and-information-security-law/texas-ag-sues-meta-over-collection-and-use-of-biometric-data), without obtaining the required consent prior to the processing.

According to the office of the Texas AG’s [press release](https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/news/releases/attorney-general-ken-paxton-secures-14-billion-settlement-meta-over-its-unauthorized-capture), the [settlement](https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/sites/default/files/images/press/Final%20State%20of%20Texas%20v%20Meta%20Order%202024.pdf) with Meta is the largest privacy settlement an Attorney General has ever obtained, signaling the Texas AG’s increased enforcement activity in the privacy space.

In 2020, Meta separately agreed to a [$650 million settlement](/privacy-and-information-security-law/texas-ag-investigates-facebooks-use-of-biometric-identifiers) of a class action brought under Illinois’ biometric privacy law.

args.summary: On July 30, 2024, Texas AG Ken Paxton announced that Meta agreed to pay $1.4 billion to settle a lawsuit over allegations that Meta processed facial geometry data of Texas residents in violation of the Texas Capture or Use of Biometric Identifier Act (CUBI). This is the first lawsuit brought and first settlement obtained under CUBI, which was passed in 2009. The lawsuit, filed in 2022, alleged Meta violated Texas law by collecting and analyzing facial geometric data for its "tag suggestions" feature without obtaining required consent. According to the Texas AG's press release, the settlement is the largest privacy settlement an Attorney General has ever obtained, signaling increased enforcement activity in the privacy space. In 2020, Meta separately agreed to a $650 million settlement of a class action under Illinois' biometric privacy law.

# Texas AG’s Billion-Dollar Settlement With Google Highlights Biometric Data Use Compliance Considerations

* Matt Fleischer-Black

  Cybersecurity Law Report

--- SOURCE 1: 2025 Illinois Compiled Statutes :: Chapter 740 - CIVIL LIABILITIES :: 740 ILCS 14/ - Biometric Information Privacy Act. ---
URL: https://law.justia.com/codes/illinois/chapter-740/act-740-ilcs-14

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage contains the full text of the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA), codified as 740 ILCS 14/, as part of the 2025 Illinois Compiled Statutes. The Act regulates the collection, use, safeguarding, handling, storage, retention, and destruction of biometric identifiers and information by private entities.

**Key provisions include:**

- **Definitions (Sec. 10):** "Biometric identifiers" include retina/iris scans, fingerprints, voiceprints, and hand/face geometry scans. Excludes writing samples, photographs, X-rays, medical images, and certain health information. "Private entity" means any individual, partnership, corporation, LLC, etc., but excludes state/local government agencies.

- **Retention, Collection, Disclosure, Destruction (Sec. 15):** Private entities must (a) develop a public written policy establishing retention schedules and destruction guidelines (within 3 years of last interaction); (b) obtain informed written consent before collecting biometric data; (c) cannot sell, lease, trade, or profit from biometric information; (d) cannot disclose biometric data without consent, except for financial transactions, legal requirements, or court orders; and (e) must store and protect biometric data using reasonable industry standards.

- **Right of Action (Sec. 20):** Any aggrieved person may sue in state circuit court or federal district court. Penalties: $1,000 liquidated damages or actual damages for negligent violations; $5,000 for intentional or reckless violations. Prevailing parties may also recover attorneys' fees, costs, and injunctive relief. The section also limits multiple recoveries for repeated violations involving the same biometric identifier and same person.

- **Construction (Sec. 25):** The Act does not apply to financial institutions subject to Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, does not conflict with HIPAA, and does not apply to contractors/subcontractors of state/local government agencies.

The Act was originally effective October 3, 2008 (P.A. 95-994), with amendments effective August 2, 2024 (P.A. 103-769).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Biometric identifier means a retina or iris scan, fingerprint, voiceprint, or scan of hand or face geometry." (Sec. 10), "No private entity in possession of a biometric identifier or biometric information may sell, lease, trade, or otherwise profit from a person's or a customer's biometric identifier or biometric information." (Sec. 15(c)), "A private entity in possession of biometric identifiers or biometric information must develop a written policy, made available to the public, establishing a retention schedule and guidelines for permanently destroying biometric identifiers and biometric information when the initial purpose for collecting or obtaining such identifiers or information has been satisfied or within 3 years of the individual's last interaction with the private entity, whichever occurs first." (Sec. 15(a)), "Any person aggrieved by a violation of this Act shall have a right of action in a State circuit court or as a supplemental claim in federal district court against an offending party." (Sec. 20(a)), "against a private entity that negligently violates a provision of this Act, liquidated damages of $1,000 or actual damages, whichever is greater" and "against a private entity that intentionally or recklessly violates a provision of this Act, liquidated damages of $5,000 or actual damages, whichever is greater" (Sec. 20(a)(1)-(2))

URL: https://www.dwt.com/blogs/privacy--security-law-blog/2024/08/illinois-bipa-biometrics-law-amended-for-damages

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a law firm blog post (from DWT) discussing the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) and a major 2024 amendment (SB 2979) that significantly limits damages. The post was originally published August 18, 2024, and updated April 20, 2026.

**Key Update (April 2026):** The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit held that the 2024 BIPA amendment applies retroactively to pending cases. The amendment clarifies that when the same biometric identifier of one individual is repeatedly collected or disclosed by the same defendant using the same method, those actions constitute a SINGLE violation for damages calculation. The court reasoned this is a remedial change, not a modification of substantive rights. This forecloses "per-scan" damages theories that multiplied potential liability.

**Original Post (August 2024):** SB 2979 was signed into law by Governor Pritzker on August 2, 2024, effective immediately. It provides that repeated collection/disclosure of the same biometric data from the same person using the same method is a single violation, entitling the person to a single damage recovery (up to $1,000 per negligent violation, $5,000 per reckless/intentional violation).

**Background:** BIPA requires notice, consent, and a written retention policy before collecting biometric data. It provides a private right of action with statutory damages. Prior to the amendment, courts awarded damages on a per-instance basis, leading to massive exposure (e.g., $228 million judgment against BNSF in Rogers, later settled for $75 million; White Castle potentially faced $17 billion in Cothron before settling for ~$10 million).

**Going Forward:** While the amendment eliminates per-scan multipliers, statutory damages of $1,000-$5,000 per individual can still produce significant exposure in class actions. The Seventh Circuit's decision provides guidance for federal courts, but the Illinois Supreme Court could ultimately revisit the retroactivity issue. Companies using biometrics must still comply with BIPA's notice, consent, and retention policy requirements.
</summary>

The amendment clarifies that when the same biometric identifier or biometric information of one individual is repeatedly collected or disclosed by the same defendant using the same method, those actions constitute a single violation for purposes of calculating statutory damages., The Seventh Circuit concluded that the amendment should be applied retroactively because it represents a remedial change to the statute rather than a modification of substantive rights., The Seventh Circuit's decision forecloses that approach by confirming that plaintiffs may recover at most one statutory damages award per person for repeated collections or disclosures involving the same biometric data and method., The new amendment reverses course from awards of potentially 'ruinous' damages that were initially recoverable for violations of BIPA., The combination of legislative and judicial developments has significantly reduced the risk of the 'per-scan' damages theories that once threatened 'ruinous' statutory damage awards.

--- SOURCE 3: Biometric Information Privacy Act - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biometric_Information_Privacy_Act

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) is an Illinois state law enacted on October 3, 2008, that regulates the collection, use, and handling of biometric identifiers and information by private entities. It does not apply to government entities. BIPA is considered the most stringent biometric privacy law in the U.S. (compared to Texas and Washington, which have similar but weaker protections).

**Key Provisions:**
- Requires companies to obtain consent before collecting or disclosing biometric identifiers
- Mandates timely destruction of biometric data
- Requires secure storage of biometric identifiers
- Entities must use a "reasonable standard of care" in managing biometric information

**Penalties:** $1,000 per violation, or $5,000 per violation if intentional or reckless. BIPA grants a private right of action, which has led to numerous class action lawsuits.

**Legislative History:** Introduced by Senator Terry Link on February 14, 2008 (SB 2400), passed both houses (113-0 House, 42-0 Senate), and signed by Governor Rod Blagojevich on October 3, 2008. A proposed federal equivalent, the National Biometric Information Privacy Act of 2020 (S. 4400), was introduced by Senator Jeff Merkley but has not passed.

**Notable Cases:**
- *In re Facebook Biometric Info. Privacy Litig.* — Facebook scanned faces without consent for Tag Suggestions; settled for $650 million in 2021
- *Monroy v. Shutterfly, Inc.* — Facial recognition scanning of uploaded photos
- *Rivera v. Google, Inc.* — Google Photos facial scans; dismissed for lack of standing
- *Rosenbach v. Six Flags Entm't Corp.* — Illinois Supreme Court ruled users need not prove actual injury to sue; mere violation is sufficient
- *McDonald v. Symphony Bronzeville Park LLC* — Nursing home collected employee biometric data without consent

**Challenges:** A 2019 bill (SB3053) sought to exempt employers from BIPA requirements but failed to pass. Privacy advocates, including the Electronic Frontier Foundation, opposed it. Facebook supported the bill, which was questioned during Mark Zuckerberg's 2018 congressional testimony.

**First Settlement:** $1.5 million against L.A. Tan Enterprises (2016), with class members receiving $125–$150 each.

**Foreign Equivalent:** The EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), effective May 25, 2018, is noted as a comparable data protection regulation.
</summary>

Privacy Litig. case, praising the settlement as 'a major win for consumers in the hotly contested area of digital privacy.'"

--- SOURCE 4: Getting BIPA Right: Biometric Identifiers Must Identify ---
URL: https://www.mofo.com/resources/insights/240503-getting-bipa-right-biometric-identifiers-must-identify

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This client alert from Morrison Foerster, dated May 6, 2024, analyzes a critical unresolved issue under the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA): whether the statute applies to biometric data that cannot identify a person. The article argues that BIPA should only regulate data capable of identifying individuals, contrary to some district court rulings.

**Key Points:**

- **Background:** BIPA (740 ILCS 14/1 et seq.) was enacted in 2008 after Pay by Touch's bankruptcy exposed risks of biometric data linked to personal information. It was designed to protect biometric data tied to identifiable individuals, not to ban biometric technology.

- **The Split:** District courts are divided. Some courts (e.g., *Colombo v. YouTube*, *Gunderson v. Amazon*) have allowed BIPA claims even where the defendant cannot identify the plaintiff from the data collected. Other courts (e.g., *Daichendt v. CVS*, *Zellmer v. Meta*) have held that BIPA requires the data to be capable of identifying a person.

- **Textual Argument:** The term "biometric identifier" inherently means something that identifies a person. The enumerated items (fingerprints, voiceprints, scans of face geometry, etc.) are defined by their use for identification. Omitting the "used to identify" clause from the definition of "biometric identifier" but including it in "biometric information" does not negate the ordinary meaning of "identifier."

- **Legislative Intent:** The General Assembly's findings (Section 5) emphasize ties to finances and personal information, and locations like grocery stores and gas stations, implying a minimum level of known contact. The Illinois Supreme Court in *Rosenbach* noted BIPA compliance should not be difficult.

- **Absurd Results:** Applying BIPA to unidentifiable data forces companies to obtain consent from total strangers, which is impossible. In *Colombo*, YouTube's face-blur feature (designed to protect privacy) was sued under BIPA, creating a net privacy loss.

- **Conclusion:** The article argues that both law and policy support limiting BIPA to data capable of identifying a person, and this issue is ripe for appellate review.
</summary>

"BIPA was designed to protect biometric data linked to individuals that posed a risk of financial or other harm if sold or disclosed.", "Some courts have concluded that BIPA applies even where there is no PII at issue... Other courts have disagreed, concluding that BIPA only applies if the data can identify an individual.", "BIPA's text and legislative history make clear that the statute seeks to protect against the collection, sale, and disclosure of biometric data 'used to identify an individual.'", "In Zellmer v. Meta, the court observed it would be 'counterintuitive' if BIPA was construed to require companies to obtain consent from individuals unknown to them.", "A fundamental principle of statutory construction is that statutes should not be interpreted in a manner that leads to 'absurd, inconvenient, [and] unjust results.'"

This article from the FORC Journal (Spring 2023) provides an update on emerging insurance issues related to the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA), enacted in 2008. BIPA regulates the collection, use, safeguarding, handling, storage, retention, and destruction of biometric identifiers (retina/iris scans, fingerprints, voiceprints, hand/face geometry). It provides for statutory damages of $1,000 for negligent violations and $5,000 for intentional violations, plus attorney fees.

Key developments covered:

2. **Workers Compensation**: In McDonald v. Symphony Bronzeville Park LLC, the Illinois Supreme Court (2022) affirmed that the exclusive remedy of Workers' Compensation does not bar BIPA claims against employers, as such claims are not compensable under the Workers' Compensation Act.

3. **General Liability Coverage**: In West Bend Mutual Ins. Co. v. Krishna Schaumburg Tan, Inc. 5. **First BIPA Class Action Trial**: In Rogers v. BNSF Railway Co. (Oct. 2022), a jury returned a $228 million verdict for approximately 45,600 reckless or intentional violations.

Insurers are increasingly excluding BIPA claims from coverage, and the article concludes that coverage availability depends on specific facts, policy language, and court interpretations.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On April 1, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit ruled in *Clay v. Union Pacific Railroad Co.* that the 2024 amendment to the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) damages provision (Section 20) applies retroactively, eliminating the possibility of "per-scan" statutory damages for cases pending at the time of enactment (Aug. 2, 2024). The amendment, P.A. 103-0769, limits plaintiffs to at most one recovery of statutory damages where the same biometric identifier is collected using the same method.

The court reasoned that the amendment affects remedies only, making it a procedural change that applies retroactively under Illinois law, rather than a substantive change to BIPA's liability standards. This decision significantly limits defendants' potential exposure in pending BIPA cases. The plaintiffs had argued they were entitled to $7.5 million individually and "billions of dollars in damages" as a class action under a per-scan interpretation.

The ruling addresses two certified questions from three consolidated district court cases (*Gregg v. Cent. Trans. LLC* and *Willis v. Universal Intermodal Servs., Inc.*): whether the amendment is a clarification applying to all pending cases, and whether it is retroactive. The Seventh Circuit held in favor of defendants on both questions.

The decision may also require district courts to reassess federal subject-matter jurisdiction, as per-scan damages were previously used to satisfy the amount-in-controversy requirement. The ruling could result in dismissal or remand of several BIPA cases to state court for lack of jurisdiction.
</summary>

The decision dramatically reduces damages exposure for employers defending BIPA claims in federal court and provides a basis for dispositive motions or enhanced settlement positions in pending cases.

Key concerns include:
- **Low hurdle to sue:** The Illinois Supreme Court's 2019 Rosenbach v. Six Flags decision found that plaintiffs need not show actual harm—mere procedural violations suffice.

This has resulted in massive settlements where attorneys receive disproportionate shares (e.g., Facebook $650M settlement with $97.5M in fees; ADP $25M settlement with $8.75M in fees).
- **Small businesses targeted:** Contrary to media reports, smaller companies face lawsuits, such as a family-run business with 65 employees and a heating/air conditioning company.
- **Lack of procedural protections:** BIPA lacks notice and cure periods, safe harbors, damage caps, and exclusive AG enforcement—all recommended protections.

The report concludes that as other states consider biometric privacy laws, BIPA should be viewed as a cautionary tale, not a blueprint.

<summary>
# Washington Biometric Privacy Law (H.B. 1493) - Summary

## Overview
The Washington Biometric Privacy Law (H.B. 1493), enacted in 2017, regulates how organizations collect, use, and store biometric identifiers of Washington state residents. The law defines a "biometric identifier" as data produced by automatic measurements of biological characteristics such as voiceprints, fingerprints, eye retinas, irises, or other unique features used to identify a specific person.

## Key Exclusions and Limitations
Privacy advocates consider Washington's law weaker than statutes in Illinois (BIPA) and Texas. Notable exclusions from the definition of biometric identifiers include:
- Physical or digital photographs, video or audio recordings, or data generated therefrom
- Scans of facial geometry (facial recognition data)
- Specific health-related data processed under HIPAA

## Notice and Consent Requirements
Organizations using biometric identifiers in a commercial setting must:
1. Provide notice to the individual
2. Obtain consent
3. Provide a mechanism to prevent subsequent use of the biometric identifier for commercial purposes

The law does not specify the exact type of notice required — it is "context-dependent." Notice must simply be "reasonably designed to be readily available to affected individuals." This contrasts sharply with Illinois' BIPA, which requires written notice and release before collection.

## Exceptions to Notice and Consent
Exemptions apply when biometric use relates to:
- A "security purpose" (broadly defined, covering misappropriation, theft, shoplifting prevention)
- Fraud prevention
- Compliance with HIPAA and Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act
- Law enforcement activities

Organizations do not need consent before leasing, disclosing, or selling biometric data if the action is: consistent with the law, part of judicial proceedings, pursuant to a court order, authorized by federal/state statute, necessary to provide a requested service, or necessary to complete a financial transaction initiated by the individual.

## Security and Retention Requirements
- Organizations must take "reasonable care" to safeguard against unauthorized acquisition or access to biometric data
- Biometric information must be retained no longer than necessary to comply with the law, protect against criminal activity, liability, security threats, fraud, or to supply the service for which the identifier was enrolled

## Enforcement — No Private Right of Action
Unlike Illinois' BIPA, Washington's law does NOT create a private right of action. Enforcement is limited to Washington's Attorney General. This means no class action lawsuits can be brought by individuals under this law.

## Compliance Recommendations
Experts recommend adopting a comprehensive framework aligned with the strictest biometric privacy laws (as suggested by the Sans Institute):
- Create a documented, comprehensive plan
- Provide a publicly available written policy (Privacy Policy) detailing: specific purposes for biometric data collection, how data will be used, how data will be disclosed and to whom, how long data will be kept and stored
- Be transparent about when and how biometric data will be destroyed
- Implement strict security protocols
- Obtain explicit consent for collection
- Include provisions in vendor contracts ensuring compliance and notification of suspected data breaches

## Practical Implementation
Businesses should disclose biometric data collection in their Privacy Policy, link the policy wherever biometric data is collected, use checkboxes to obtain consent, and maintain records of consent to prove compliance.
</summary>

# Washington State Chapter 19.375 RCW: Biometric Identifiers

This chapter of the Washington State Revised Code (RCW), enacted in 2017, regulates the use of biometric identifiers for commercial purposes. It establishes requirements for businesses regarding enrollment, disclosure, retention, and security of biometric data.

## Key Definitions

- **Biometric identifier**: Data generated from automatic measurements of biological characteristics (fingerprints, voiceprints, retinas, irises, etc.) used to identify a specific individual. Excludes photographs, video/audio recordings, and HIPAA-related health information.
- **Biometric system**: An automated identification system that captures, processes, stores, compares, and matches biometric identifiers.
- **Enroll**: To capture a biometric identifier, convert it into a non-reconstructable reference template, and store it in a database.
- **Commercial purpose**: Purpose related to selling or disclosing biometric identifiers to third parties for marketing goods/services unrelated to the initial transaction (excludes security or law enforcement purposes).

## Core Requirements (Section 19.375.020)

### Notice and Consent
- Businesses cannot enroll biometric identifiers for commercial purposes without providing notice, obtaining consent, or offering a mechanism to prevent subsequent commercial use.
- Notice and consent requirements are context-dependent.

### Disclosure Restrictions
Without individual consent, a person who has enrolled a biometric identifier cannot sell, lease, or disclose it for commercial purposes unless:
- Consistent with notice/consent requirements
- Necessary to provide a requested product/service
- Required for a financial transaction the individual authorized
- Required by law or court order
- Made to a third party who contractually promises confidentiality
- For litigation preparation or judicial process participation

### Security and Retention
- Must take reasonable care to guard against unauthorized access
- May retain biometric identifiers only as long as reasonably necessary for legal compliance, fraud prevention, or providing the enrolled services

### Material Changes
- Cannot use or disclose biometric identifiers in a materially inconsistent manner from the original terms without obtaining new consent

## Enforcement (Section 19.375.030)
- Violations are considered unfair or deceptive acts under the Consumer Protection Act (Chapter 19.86 RCW)
- Enforcement is solely by the Attorney General (no private right of action)

## Exclusions (Section 19.375.040)
- Financial institutions subject to Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act
- Activities subject to HIPAA
- Law enforcement officers acting within their authority

## Legislative Intent (Section 19.375.900)
The legislature found that Washington citizens are increasingly asked to disclose sensitive biological information, and the collection/marketing of biometric data without consent is of increasing concern. The law aims to require businesses to disclose how they use biometric data and obtain consent before enrolling or changing the use of biometric identifiers.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Washington Biometric Privacy Protection Act (House Bill 1493), passed in May 2017, regulates how businesses collect and use biometric information for commercial purposes in Washington State. It prohibits enrolling a biometric identifier in a database for commercial purposes without providing notice, obtaining consent, or offering a mechanism to prevent subsequent use. "Biometric identifier" is defined as data generated by automatic measurements of biological characteristics (fingerprint, voiceprint, retina/iris patterns, etc.) used to identify a specific individual, but excludes photographs, video, or audio recordings. The law applies to all individuals and non-government entities collecting biometric identifiers, except those using them for security purposes.

**Key Requirements:**
- Provide notice before collecting biometric information
- Cannot use or disclose biometric data in ways materially inconsistent with the original terms of consent
- Must maintain safeguards at least as protective as those used for other confidential information
- Cannot sell, lease, or disclose biometric identifiers without consent, except where necessary for a requested product/service or to a third party contractually promising limited use

The law is enforced by the Washington State Attorney General with no private right of action under the statute itself, though violations are treated as unfair or deceptive acts under the Washington Consumer Protection Act (CPA), which does allow individuals to sue for damages. The law requires biometric data be destroyed within a reasonable time after it has served its purpose or within three years of the individual's last interaction, whichever is earlier. Businesses must obtain explicit informed consent detailing the purpose, use, and retention duration of data collection. The Act is similar to Illinois' BIPA but includes specific data retention/destruction provisions and clearer security guidelines.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: Washington Biometric Privacy Law (H.B. 1493) ---
URL: https://www.termsfeed.com/blog/washington-biometric-privacy-law-hb-1493

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Washington Biometric Privacy Law (H.B. 1493) - Summary

## Overview
The Washington Biometric Privacy Law (H.B. 1493), enacted in 2017, regulates how organizations collect, use, and store biometric identifiers of Washington state residents. The law defines a "biometric identifier" as data produced by automatic measurements of biological characteristics such as voiceprints, fingerprints, eye retinas, irises, or other unique features used to identify a specific person.

## Key Exclusions and Limitations
Privacy advocates consider Washington's law weaker than statutes in Illinois (BIPA) and Texas. Notable exclusions from the definition of biometric identifiers include:
- Physical or digital photographs, video or audio recordings, or data generated therefrom
- Scans of facial geometry (facial recognition data)
- Specific health-related data processed under HIPAA

## Notice and Consent Requirements
Organizations using biometric identifiers in a commercial setting must:
1. Provide notice to the individual
2. Obtain consent
3. Provide a mechanism to prevent subsequent use of the biometric identifier for commercial purposes

The law does not specify the exact type of notice required — it is "context-dependent." Notice must simply be "reasonably designed to be readily available to affected individuals." This contrasts sharply with Illinois' BIPA, which requires written notice and release before collection.

## Exceptions to Notice and Consent
Exemptions apply when biometric use relates to:
- A "security purpose" (broadly defined, covering misappropriation, theft, shoplifting prevention)
- Fraud prevention
- Compliance with HIPAA and Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act
- Law enforcement activities

Organizations do not need consent before leasing, disclosing, or selling biometric data if the action is: consistent with the law, part of judicial proceedings, pursuant to a court order, authorized by federal/state statute, necessary to provide a requested service, or necessary to complete a financial transaction initiated by the individual.

## Security and Retention Requirements
- Organizations must take "reasonable care" to safeguard against unauthorized acquisition or access to biometric data
- Biometric information must be retained no longer than necessary to comply with the law, protect against criminal activity, liability, security threats, fraud, or to supply the service for which the identifier was enrolled

## Enforcement — No Private Right of Action
Unlike Illinois' BIPA, Washington's law does NOT create a private right of action. Enforcement is limited to Washington's Attorney General. This means no class action lawsuits can be brought by individuals under this law.

## Compliance Recommendations
Experts recommend adopting a comprehensive framework aligned with the strictest biometric privacy laws (as suggested by the Sans Institute):
- Create a documented, comprehensive plan
- Provide a publicly available written policy (Privacy Policy) detailing: specific purposes for biometric data collection, how data will be used, how data will be disclosed and to whom, how long data will be kept and stored
- Be transparent about when and how biometric data will be destroyed
- Implement strict security protocols
- Obtain explicit consent for collection
- Include provisions in vendor contracts ensuring compliance and notification of suspected data breaches

## Practical Implementation
Businesses should disclose biometric data collection in their Privacy Policy, link the policy wherever biometric data is collected, use checkboxes to obtain consent, and maintain records of consent to prove compliance.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Washington State My Health My Data Act ---
URL: https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/FPF-Legislation-Policy-Brief_-The-Washington-My-Health-My-Data-Act-Public-Version.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Washington State 'My Health, My Data' Act (MHMD) is a comprehensive consumer privacy law signed by Governor Inslee on April 27, 2023, designed to protect consumer health data not covered by HIPAA. It was motivated partly by the Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization Supreme Court decision and aims to protect individuals seeking reproductive health and gender-affirming care. MHMD is arguably the furthest-reaching state consumer privacy law enacted in the U.S.

**Key Provisions:**
- **Broad Definition of "Consumer Health Data":** Covers physical and mental health "status" with a non-exhaustive list of 13 categories, including precise geolocation data (within 1,750 feet) that could indicate attempts to receive health services, biometric data, genetic data, gender-affirming care information, reproductive/sexual health information, and even data identifying a consumer seeking health care services (which could impact search engines and AI chatbots).
- **Prescriptive Consent Requirements:** Requires separate consumer consent for "collection" and "sharing" of health data (unless necessary to provide a requested product/service), plus a heightened "valid authorization" for "sale" of health data. Consent must be a clear affirmative act, and "deceptive design" is prohibited. Notably, the definition of "deceptive design" lacks a "substantial effect" requirement found in other state laws.
- **Expansive Consumer Rights:** Grants rights to confirm processing, access health data, and delete health data across all records (including archived/backup systems with a possible 6-month delay). Consumers can also access lists of third parties and affiliates with whom data was shared or sold. Notably, there is no right to correct inaccurate data.
- **Geofencing Restrictions:** Forbids implementing a geofence (virtual boundary of 2,000 feet or less) around health care facilities to identify/track consumers, collect health data, or send notifications/advertisements related to health data.
- **Private Right of Action:** Violations are treated as unfair or deceptive trade practices under the Washington Consumer Protection Act (WCPA), allowing both AG enforcement and private lawsuits. Consumers may recover actual damages, with courts having discretion to award treble damages up to $25,000.
- **Coverage:** Applies to "regulated entities" doing business in Washington or targeting Washington consumers. Has broad extraterritorial effect due to defining "collect" as processing in "any manner." Few entity-level carve-outs exist (small businesses, nonprofits, universities, HIPAA/GLBA entities are covered, though data-level exemptions exist). Government "agencies" are exempt, but not other government bodies.
- **Effective Dates:** Data privacy provisions take effect March 31, 2024 (June 30, 2024 for small businesses); geofencing and enforcement provisions take effect July 22, 2023.
- **Data-Level Exemptions:** Exists for information protected under HIPAA, GLBA, Social Security Act, FCRA, and FERPA. Also exempts data used for public health activities and public interest research.
- **Notable Omissions:** No common exceptions for complying with legal obligations/responding to legal process, no non-retaliation exemption for bona fide loyalty programs, and no prohibition against unlawful discrimination in processing health data.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Debevoise Data Blog (published October 19, 2021) is Part 1 of a two-part series analyzing the legal landscape for facial recognition technology in the United States. It explains the tension between companies adopting facial recognition tools and legislatures pushing back with privacy restrictions.

**Key Uses of Facial Recognition:** User authentication, security authorization (e.g., casinos identifying cheaters, stores identifying shoplifters), marketing, general surveillance (including employer productivity tracking), law enforcement, assistive technology for the blind, and digital doorbells.

**Current Legal Patchwork:** There is no single comprehensive U.S. facial recognition law. The framework consists of:

1. **State Biometric Privacy Laws:**
   - **Illinois (BIPA)** – Enacted 2008, requires written retention/destruction policies, notice and written consent, prohibits selling/profiting from biometric data, limits disclosure, and imposes a duty of care. Provides a private right of action with statutory damages. Has generated significant class actions (e.g., $650M Facebook settlement, $36M Six Flags settlement).
   - **Washington** – Excludes biometrics derived from photos/videos, only applies to "enrolled" identifiers, provides safe harbor for security purposes, does not require written consent, and is enforceable only by the state attorney general.
   - **Texas** – Similar to BIPA but consent can be in any form (not necessarily written), enforceable only by the state attorney general with civil penalties capped at $25,000 per violation.

2. **Municipal Bans:** Cities including San Francisco, Oakland, Boston, Portland (OR), Minneapolis, and New Orleans have banned government use of facial recognition. Portland (OR) and Baltimore also restrict private sector use. Portland's ordinance bans private entities from using facial recognition within city limits with exceptions for device security (e.g., FaceID) and social media apps.

3. **New York City Regulations:** Requires commercial establishments to post notices about biometric data collection and bans profiting from biometric identifier information. The Tenant Data Privacy Act regulates landlords' use of smart access systems collecting biometric data.

4. **General Privacy Laws:** California (CCPA/CPRA), Virginia (VCDPA), and Colorado (CPA) include biometrics as "sensitive personal information," requiring consent for processing.

5. **Data Breach Notification:** About 20 states (including CA, IL, NY, WA) have added biometric identifiers as triggers for breach notification.

6. **Reasonable Security Requirements:** About 25 states require reasonable security measures for biometric data.

The article notes that the most restrictive regulations have come from city councils, with bans based on evidence that facial recognition can have disproportionate adverse impacts on marginalized communities, including bias against women and people of color.
</summary>

"Two huge crosscurrents are sweeping the world of facial recognition—and moving head-on into each other. Companies are eagerly adopting facial recognition tools... Meanwhile, legislatures and privacy advocates are pushing back hard.", "The most restrictive regulations on facial recognition in the United States have come from city councils. Across the country, municipalities have passed laws banning the use of facial recognition technologies by state and local agencies, especially police departments.", "Legislative bodies have noted evidence that facial recognition technologies can have a disproportionate and adverse impact on marginalized communities, including due to bias in their ability to correctly identify women and people of color.", "The Illinois Supreme Court has ruled that a plaintiff does not need to show real-world harm to state a successful claim—that is, a violation of the statute is enough.", "Unsurprisingly, BIPA has begun to generate significant class action litigation both in Illinois and elsewhere: The Six Flags case... resulted in a $36 million settlement. ... SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage contains the text of Texas Business and Commerce Code § 503.001, which regulates the capture or use of biometric identifiers for commercial purposes. Key provisions include:

- **Biometric identifier** is defined as a retina or iris scan, fingerprint, voiceprint, or record of hand or face geometry.
- **Consent requirement**: A person may not capture a biometric identifier for a commercial purpose unless they inform the individual beforehand and receive consent. Consent is not implied merely by the existence of an image or media on the internet or public sources, unless the individual themselves made it public.
- **Restrictions on disclosure**: Possessors of biometric identifiers cannot sell, lease, or disclose them except under specific circumstances (e.g., individual consents for identification in case of disappearance/death, to complete a requested financial transaction, as required by federal/state law, or to law enforcement via warrant).
- **Security and destruction**: Biometric identifiers must be stored, transmitted, and protected with reasonable care (at least as protective as other confidential information). They must be destroyed within one year after the purpose for collection expires (or within one year after a required instrument/document is no longer legally required to be maintained). For employer-collected security purposes, the purpose expires upon termination of employment.
- **Penalties**: Violations are subject to a civil penalty of up to $25,000 per violation, enforceable by the Texas Attorney General.
- **Exemptions**: The section does not apply to (1) voiceprint data held by financial institutions/affiliates (per 15 U.S.C. § 6809); (2) training, processing, or storage of biometric identifiers for developing/training AI models or systems, unless the system is used to uniquely identify a specific individual; and (3) developing/deploying AI for security, fraud prevention, system integrity, or investigating illegal activities.
- **Subsequent commercial use**: If a biometric identifier captured for AI training is later used for a commercial purpose not covered by the exemptions, the possessor becomes subject to the possession/destruction requirements and penalties of this section.

This article by Nikolay Sapunov (CEO of Fora Soft) provides engineering guidance on US biometric privacy law as it applies to video surveillance systems. The key message is that the US has no federal biometric law; instead, it has a patchwork of state-level regulations. The most consequential is Illinois's Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA, 740 ILCS 14), because it is the only one that provides a private right of action—allowing individuals to sue directly with fixed damages of $1,000 (negligent) or $5,000 (reckless/intentional) per person, with no need to prove harm.

**Three layers of US regulation:**
1. **Three dedicated biometric statute states:** Illinois (BIPA), Texas (CUBI), Washington (RCW 19.375)—all require consent before capture
2. **~20 comprehensive privacy laws** treating biometrics as "sensitive data" requiring opt-in consent (e.g., California, Colorado, Virginia)
3. **Everything else** (FTC authority, sector rules)

**Critical distinction:** Recording video is not regulated—building a faceprint (template) from it is. BIPA defines a "biometric identifier" as a retina/iris scan, fingerprint, voiceprint, or scan of face geometry (faceprint). Photographs are explicitly excluded.

**BIPA's core duties (Section 15):**
- 15(b): Written notice + signed release BEFORE capture (structurally impossible in open public space)
- 15(a): Written public retention/destruction policy—destroy within 3 years of last interaction
- 15(c): No selling biometric data
- 15(d): No disclosure without consent
- 15(e): Reasonable security standard

**Why Illinois is uniquely dangerous:** 
- *Rosenbach v. Six Flags (2019)*: No proof of harm needed to sue
- *Cothron v. White Castle (2023)*: Originally allowed per-scan claims; 2024 amendment (SB 2979) capped same-person/same-method to single recovery
- Real settlements: Facebook $650M (2021), Clearview AI equity ~$51.75M (2025), Texas AG settled with Meta for $1.4B (2024)

**Engineering recommendations:** Biometric analytics as gated feature (off by default), geo-fence by state, enforce destruction clocks, use detection-only pipelines where possible to avoid biometric statutes entirely.

Symphony* (2022) - employees can sue employers; *Cothron* (2023) - each scan/transmission is a separate violation; *Tims* (2023) - 5-year statute of limitations. These decisions caused a 1400% increase in BIPA lawsuits (9 in 2018 to 134 in 2019).

**Enforcement:** Texas was relatively inactive until 2022 when the AG filed major lawsuits against Google and Meta, seeking billions in damages.

**Other States:** Only 3 states (Illinois, Texas, Washington) have active biometric privacy legislation. New York City has a disclosure ordinance. A federal "National Biometric Information Privacy Act of 2020" was proposed but not advanced.

This article, published on January 28, 2021 by Segal McCambridge Singer & Mahoney, provides a comprehensive overview of Texas' biometric law (CUBI) and compares it to biometric privacy laws across other U.S. states.

No private right of action; Attorney General can seek penalties up to $5,000 or $20 per instance (cap $250,000).

--- SOURCE 18: A BAD MATCH: ILLINOIS AND THE BIOMETRIC ... ---
URL: https://instituteforlegalreform.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/ILR-BIPA-Briefly-FINAL.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This October 2021 ILR Briefly report argues that the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) is a prime example of a misdirected law that has led to more litigation abuse than consumer protection. Enacted in 2008, BIPA regulates the collection, retention, and disclosure of biometric identifiers and is the only state biometric privacy law (among Illinois, Texas, and Washington) that authorizes a private right of action (PRA).

Key concerns include:
- **Low hurdle to sue:** The Illinois Supreme Court's 2019 Rosenbach v. Six Flags decision found that plaintiffs need not show actual harm—mere procedural violations suffice.
- **Exponential litigation growth:** From only 15 BIPA class actions filed between 2008-2016, litigation surged to nearly 300 cases in Illinois in 2019 alone. Through September 2021, over 900 BIPA cases had been filed.
- **Uncapped damages and attorneys' fees:** BIPA allows liquidated damages of $1,000 (negligent) or $5,000 (intentional/reckless) per violation, with uncapped attorneys' fees. This has resulted in massive settlements where attorneys receive disproportionate shares (e.g., Facebook $650M settlement with $97.5M in fees; ADP $25M settlement with $8.75M in fees).
- **Small businesses targeted:** Contrary to media reports, smaller companies face lawsuits, such as a family-run business with 65 employees and a heating/air conditioning company.
- **Lack of procedural protections:** BIPA lacks notice and cure periods, safe harbors, damage caps, and exclusive AG enforcement—all recommended protections.

The report concludes that as other states consider biometric privacy laws, BIPA should be viewed as a cautionary tale, not a blueprint.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Squire Patton Boggs' Privacy World blog reviews 2025 developments in biometric privacy litigation, with a focus on Illinois' Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) and other state laws. Key points include:

**BIPA Background:** Enacted in 2008, BIPA requires notice and consent before collecting biometric data, with a private right of action allowing statutory damages of $1,000 for negligent violations and $5,000 for willful misconduct. A 2024 amendment limited recovery to one violation per aggrieved party.

**2025 Class Action & Mass Arbitration Activity:** At least 100 putative BIPA class actions were filed in 2025. High-value settlements were reached, and contested class certifications were granted. BIPA also became a staple of mass arbitration claims, with plaintiffs' firms recruiting claimants online across various industries.

**Seventh Circuit Appeals:** Two key BIPA exemption issues are pending before the Seventh Circuit: (1) the GLBA Exemption in Cisneros v. Nuance Communications, where oral argument was heard in October 2025; and (2) the Government Contractor Exemption in Payton v. Union Pacific Railroad, where an interlocutory appeal was certified.

**NYC Biometric Law:** A federal court in Schottenstein (Dec. 2025) dismissed a claim under New York City's biometric law, holding it is "meaningfully different" from BIPA—it prohibits profiting from a transaction of biometric information, not merely from the information itself.

**AG Enforcement:** Colorado's H.B. 24-1130 went into effect July 1, 2025, requiring employer biometric policies and consent. Texas secured a $1.375 billion settlement with Google, including for alleged violations of the Texas Capture or Use of Biometric Identifier Act (CUBI), which allows $25,000 per violation.

**AI & Biometrics:** Three notable 2025 decisions: (1) A court approved a settlement where an AI startup gave plaintiffs a 23% stake in the company for building a facial recognition database; (2) A New Jersey federal court held that AI is not a "medical professional" and cannot provide treatment under BIPA's medical exception; (3) A New York federal court found that creating AI voice clones of voice actors without consent violated New York Civil Rights Law.

URL: https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/88R/billtext/html/HB04705I.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is Texas House Bill No. 4705, the "Biometric Data Privacy Act of 2023," which amends Chapter 503 of the Texas Business and Commerce Code to regulate the collection, use, safeguarding, handling, storage, retention, and destruction of biometric identifiers and biometric information. The bill defines "biometric identifier" to include retina or iris scans, palm or vascular vein patterns, heartbeat, fingerprints, voiceprints, key strokes, signature, gait, and hand or face geometry (excluding digital/physical photographs and audio/video recordings unless used to identify a specific individual). 

Key provisions include:
- A person may not capture biometric identifiers/information for a commercial purpose without first: (1) informing the individual in writing that the data is being collected/stored; (2) informing them of the specific purpose and retention term; and (3) obtaining a written release.
- Prohibits selling, leasing, trading, or disclosing biometric data unless the individual consents (for identification in case of death/disappearance), the disclosure completes a requested financial transaction, is required by statute, or is made to a law enforcement agency pursuant to a warrant or subpoena.
- Requires storage, transmission, and protection of biometric data using reasonable care, at least as protective as other confidential information.
- Mandates permanent destruction of biometric data within one year of the purpose for collection expiring (or within one year after a related legal document is no longer required to be maintained).
- For employer-collected biometric data for security purposes, the purpose is presumed to expire upon termination of employment.
- Violations are subject to a civil penalty of up to $25,000 per violation, enforceable by the Texas Attorney General or an affected individual.
- Exempts voiceprint data retained by financial institutions or their affiliates (as defined by 15 U.S.C. § 6809).
- The Act took effect on September 1, 2023, and applies only to violations occurring on or after that date.
</summary>

Texas is a U.S. state in the Southern United States, nicknamed the "Lone Star State" for the single star on its flag, symbolizing its former status as the independent Republic of Texas. It is the second-largest U.S. state by both area (268,596 sq mi) and population (estimated 31.7 million residents in 2025). Texas borders Louisiana, Arkansas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Mexican states along the Rio Grande, and the Gulf of Mexico.

Spain first claimed Texas, followed by French colonization, then Mexican rule after 1821. Tensions led to the Texas Revolution (including the Battle of the Alamo) and the Republic of Texas in 1836. This law review article examines the conflict between Article III standing requirements in federal courts and class action lawsuits brought under Illinois's Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA). BIPA regulates the collection, retention, disclosure, and destruction of biometric identifiers (fingerprints, facial geometry, etc.) and provides a private right of action. While Illinois state courts recognize any BIPA violation as sufficient injury, federal courts require concrete harm under Article III, creating a jurisdictional battleground.

The article analyzes five BIPA sections: §15(a) (failure to publish retention/destruction policies), §15(b) (collection without consent), §15(c) (profiting from biometric data), §15(d) (unauthorized disclosure), and §15(e) (failure to use reasonable care). Courts generally view §15(b), (d), and (e) as creating concrete harm, while §15(a) and (c) are often treated as procedural violations requiring additional injury for standing.

The article proposes a two-tiered analysis: (1) violations of §15(b), (d), and (e) should be analogized to invasion of privacy, and (2) violations of §15(a) and (c) should be analogized to the common law tort of conversion. It discusses key cases including Rosenbach v. Six Flags, Patel v. Facebook ($650 million settlement), Bryant v. Compass Group, Fox v. Dakkota, and Thornley v. Clearview AI. The article also addresses the tension between class certification requirements under Rule 23 and Article III standing, particularly after the Supreme Court's decisions in Spokeo v. Robins (2016) and TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez (2021), which held that statutory violations alone do not confer standing and that all class members must demonstrate concrete injury.

--- SOURCE 1: 2025 Illinois Compiled Statutes :: Chapter 740 - CIVIL LIABILITIES :: 740 ILCS 14/ - Biometric Information Privacy Act. ---
URL: https://law.justia.com/codes/illinois/chapter-740/act-740-ilcs-14

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage contains the full text of the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA), codified as 740 ILCS 14/, as part of the 2025 Illinois Compiled Statutes. The Act regulates the collection, use, safeguarding, handling, storage, retention, and destruction of biometric identifiers and information by private entities.

**Key provisions include:**

- **Definitions (Sec. 10):** "Biometric identifiers" include retina/iris scans, fingerprints, voiceprints, and hand/face geometry scans. Excludes writing samples, photographs, X-rays, medical images, and certain health information. "Private entity" means any individual, partnership, corporation, LLC, etc., but excludes state/local government agencies.

- **Retention, Collection, Disclosure, Destruction (Sec. 15):** Private entities must (a) develop a public written policy establishing retention schedules and destruction guidelines (within 3 years of last interaction); (b) obtain informed written consent before collecting biometric data; (c) cannot sell, lease, trade, or profit from biometric information; (d) cannot disclose biometric data without consent, except for financial transactions, legal requirements, or court orders; and (e) must store and protect biometric data using reasonable industry standards.

- **Right of Action (Sec. 20):** Any aggrieved person may sue in state circuit court or federal district court. Penalties: $1,000 liquidated damages or actual damages for negligent violations; $5,000 for intentional or reckless violations. Prevailing parties may also recover attorneys' fees, costs, and injunctive relief. The section also limits multiple recoveries for repeated violations involving the same biometric identifier and same person.

- **Construction (Sec. 25):** The Act does not apply to financial institutions subject to Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, does not conflict with HIPAA, and does not apply to contractors/subcontractors of state/local government agencies.

The Act was originally effective October 3, 2008 (P.A. 95-994), with amendments effective August 2, 2024 (P.A. 103-769).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Biometric identifier means a retina or iris scan, fingerprint, voiceprint, or scan of hand or face geometry." (Sec. 10), "No private entity in possession of a biometric identifier or biometric information may sell, lease, trade, or otherwise profit from a person's or a customer's biometric identifier or biometric information." (Sec. 15(c)), "A private entity in possession of biometric identifiers or biometric information must develop a written policy, made available to the public, establishing a retention schedule and guidelines for permanently destroying biometric identifiers and biometric information when the initial purpose for collecting or obtaining such identifiers or information has been satisfied or within 3 years of the individual's last interaction with the private entity, whichever occurs first." (Sec. 15(a)), "Any person aggrieved by a violation of this Act shall have a right of action in a State circuit court or as a supplemental claim in federal district court against an offending party." (Sec. 20(a)), "against a private entity that negligently violates a provision of this Act, liquidated damages of $1,000 or actual damages, whichever is greater" and "against a private entity that intentionally or recklessly violates a provision of this Act, liquidated damages of $5,000 or actual damages, whichever is greater" (Sec. 20(a)(1)-(2))

--- SOURCE 2: UPDATE: Seventh Circuit Holds That BIPA Amendment Limiting Damages Applies Retroactively | Davis Wright Tremaine ---
URL: https://www.dwt.com/blogs/privacy--security-law-blog/2024/08/illinois-bipa-biometrics-law-amended-for-damages

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a law firm blog post (from DWT) discussing the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) and a major 2024 amendment (SB 2979) that significantly limits damages. The post was originally published August 18, 2024, and updated April 20, 2026.

**Key Update (April 2026):** The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit held that the 2024 BIPA amendment applies retroactively to pending cases. The amendment clarifies that when the same biometric identifier of one individual is repeatedly collected or disclosed by the same defendant using the same method, those actions constitute a SINGLE violation for damages calculation. The court reasoned this is a remedial change, not a modification of substantive rights. This forecloses "per-scan" damages theories that multiplied potential liability.

**Original Post (August 2024):** SB 2979 was signed into law by Governor Pritzker on August 2, 2024, effective immediately. It provides that repeated collection/disclosure of the same biometric data from the same person using the same method is a single violation, entitling the person to a single damage recovery (up to $1,000 per negligent violation, $5,000 per reckless/intentional violation).

**Background:** BIPA requires notice, consent, and a written retention policy before collecting biometric data. It provides a private right of action with statutory damages. Prior to the amendment, courts awarded damages on a per-instance basis, leading to massive exposure (e.g., $228 million judgment against BNSF in Rogers, later settled for $75 million; White Castle potentially faced $17 billion in Cothron before settling for ~$10 million).

**Going Forward:** While the amendment eliminates per-scan multipliers, statutory damages of $1,000-$5,000 per individual can still produce significant exposure in class actions. The Seventh Circuit's decision provides guidance for federal courts, but the Illinois Supreme Court could ultimately revisit the retroactivity issue. Companies using biometrics must still comply with BIPA's notice, consent, and retention policy requirements.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The amendment clarifies that when the same biometric identifier or biometric information of one individual is repeatedly collected or disclosed by the same defendant using the same method, those actions constitute a single violation for purposes of calculating statutory damages., The Seventh Circuit concluded that the amendment should be applied retroactively because it represents a remedial change to the statute rather than a modification of substantive rights., The Seventh Circuit's decision forecloses that approach by confirming that plaintiffs may recover at most one statutory damages award per person for repeated collections or disclosures involving the same biometric data and method., The new amendment reverses course from awards of potentially 'ruinous' damages that were initially recoverable for violations of BIPA., The combination of legislative and judicial developments has significantly reduced the risk of the 'per-scan' damages theories that once threatened 'ruinous' statutory damage awards.

--- SOURCE 3: Biometric Information Privacy Act - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biometric_Information_Privacy_Act

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) is an Illinois state law enacted on October 3, 2008, that regulates the collection, use, and handling of biometric identifiers and information by private entities. It does not apply to government entities. BIPA is considered the most stringent biometric privacy law in the U.S. (compared to Texas and Washington, which have similar but weaker protections).

**Key Provisions:**
- Requires companies to obtain consent before collecting or disclosing biometric identifiers
- Mandates timely destruction of biometric data
- Requires secure storage of biometric identifiers
- Entities must use a "reasonable standard of care" in managing biometric information

**Penalties:** $1,000 per violation, or $5,000 per violation if intentional or reckless. BIPA grants a private right of action, which has led to numerous class action lawsuits.

**Legislative History:** Introduced by Senator Terry Link on February 14, 2008 (SB 2400), passed both houses (113-0 House, 42-0 Senate), and signed by Governor Rod Blagojevich on October 3, 2008. A proposed federal equivalent, the National Biometric Information Privacy Act of 2020 (S. 4400), was introduced by Senator Jeff Merkley but has not passed.

**Notable Cases:**
- *In re Facebook Biometric Info. Privacy Litig.* — Facebook scanned faces without consent for Tag Suggestions; settled for $650 million in 2021
- *Monroy v. Shutterfly, Inc.* — Facial recognition scanning of uploaded photos
- *Rivera v. Google, Inc.* — Google Photos facial scans; dismissed for lack of standing
- *Rosenbach v. Six Flags Entm't Corp.* — Illinois Supreme Court ruled users need not prove actual injury to sue; mere violation is sufficient
- *McDonald v. Symphony Bronzeville Park LLC* — Nursing home collected employee biometric data without consent

**Challenges:** A 2019 bill (SB3053) sought to exempt employers from BIPA requirements but failed to pass. Privacy advocates, including the Electronic Frontier Foundation, opposed it. Facebook supported the bill, which was questioned during Mark Zuckerberg's 2018 congressional testimony.

**First Settlement:** $1.5 million against L.A. Tan Enterprises (2016), with class members receiving $125–$150 each.

**Foreign Equivalent:** The EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), effective May 25, 2018, is noted as a comparable data protection regulation.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Getting BIPA Right: Biometric Identifiers Must Identify ---
URL: https://www.mofo.com/resources/insights/240503-getting-bipa-right-biometric-identifiers-must-identify

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This client alert from Morrison Foerster, dated May 6, 2024, analyzes a critical unresolved issue under the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA): whether the statute applies to biometric data that cannot identify a person. The article argues that BIPA should only regulate data capable of identifying individuals, contrary to some district court rulings.

**Key Points:**

- **Background:** BIPA (740 ILCS 14/1 et seq.) was enacted in 2008 after Pay by Touch's bankruptcy exposed risks of biometric data linked to personal information. It was designed to protect biometric data tied to identifiable individuals, not to ban biometric technology.

- **The Split:** District courts are divided. Some courts (e.g., *Colombo v. YouTube*, *Gunderson v. Amazon*) have allowed BIPA claims even where the defendant cannot identify the plaintiff from the data collected. Other courts (e.g., *Daichendt v. CVS*, *Zellmer v. Meta*) have held that BIPA requires the data to be capable of identifying a person.

- **Textual Argument:** The term "biometric identifier" inherently means something that identifies a person. The enumerated items (fingerprints, voiceprints, scans of face geometry, etc.) are defined by their use for identification. Omitting the "used to identify" clause from the definition of "biometric identifier" but including it in "biometric information" does not negate the ordinary meaning of "identifier."

- **Legislative Intent:** The General Assembly's findings (Section 5) emphasize ties to finances and personal information, and locations like grocery stores and gas stations, implying a minimum level of known contact. The Illinois Supreme Court in *Rosenbach* noted BIPA compliance should not be difficult.

- **Absurd Results:** Applying BIPA to unidentifiable data forces companies to obtain consent from total strangers, which is impossible. In *Colombo*, YouTube's face-blur feature (designed to protect privacy) was sued under BIPA, creating a net privacy loss.

- **Conclusion:** The article argues that both law and policy support limiting BIPA to data capable of identifying a person, and this issue is ripe for appellate review.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"BIPA was designed to protect biometric data linked to individuals that posed a risk of financial or other harm if sold or disclosed.", "Some courts have concluded that BIPA applies even where there is no PII at issue... Other courts have disagreed, concluding that BIPA only applies if the data can identify an individual.", "BIPA's text and legislative history make clear that the statute seeks to protect against the collection, sale, and disclosure of biometric data 'used to identify an individual.'", "In Zellmer v. Meta, the court observed it would be 'counterintuitive' if BIPA was construed to require companies to obtain consent from individuals unknown to them.", "A fundamental principle of statutory construction is that statutes should not be interpreted in a manner that leads to 'absurd, inconvenient, [and] unjust results.'"
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:

This article from the FORC Journal (Spring 2023) provides an update on emerging insurance issues related to the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA), enacted in 2008. BIPA regulates the collection, use, safeguarding, handling, storage, retention, and destruction of biometric identifiers (retina/iris scans, fingerprints, voiceprints, hand/face geometry). It provides for statutory damages of $1,000 for negligent violations and $5,000 for intentional violations, plus attorney fees.

Key developments covered:

1. **Six Flags and Standing**: In Rosenbach v. Six Flags Entm't Corp. (2019), the Illinois Supreme Court held that a person need not sustain actual damages beyond a violation of their rights under BIPA to bring an action.

2. **Workers Compensation**: In McDonald v. Symphony Bronzeville Park LLC, the Illinois Supreme Court (2022) affirmed that the exclusive remedy of Workers' Compensation does not bar BIPA claims against employers, as such claims are not compensable under the Workers' Compensation Act.

5. **First BIPA Class Action Trial**: In Rogers v. BNSF Railway Co. (Oct. 2022), a jury returned a $228 million verdict for approximately 45,600 reckless or intentional violations.

Insurers are increasingly excluding BIPA claims from coverage, and the article concludes that coverage availability depends on specific facts, policy language, and court interpretations.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On April 1, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit ruled in *Clay v. Union Pacific Railroad Co.* that the 2024 amendment to the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) damages provision (Section 20) applies retroactively, eliminating the possibility of "per-scan" statutory damages for cases pending at the time of enactment (Aug. 2, 2024). The amendment, P.A. 103-0769, limits plaintiffs to at most one recovery of statutory damages where the same biometric identifier is collected using the same method.

The court reasoned that the amendment affects remedies only, making it a procedural change that applies retroactively under Illinois law, rather than a substantive change to BIPA's liability standards. This decision significantly limits defendants' potential exposure in pending BIPA cases. The plaintiffs had argued they were entitled to $7.5 million individually and "billions of dollars in damages" as a class action under a per-scan interpretation.

The ruling addresses two certified questions from three consolidated district court cases (*Gregg v. Cent. Trans. LLC* and *Willis v. Universal Intermodal Servs., Inc.*): whether the amendment is a clarification applying to all pending cases, and whether it is retroactive. The Seventh Circuit held in favor of defendants on both questions.

The decision may also require district courts to reassess federal subject-matter jurisdiction, as per-scan damages were previously used to satisfy the amount-in-controversy requirement. The ruling could result in dismissal or remand of several BIPA cases to state court for lack of jurisdiction.
</summary>

If the amendment does not apply, each plaintiff argues he is entitled to a substantial award of damages.'", "The plaintiffs argued that under their interpretation of the statute, they were entitled to $7.5 million in statutory damages for their individual claim and 'billions of dollars in damages' in the case brought as a putative class action."
