**PART 4: PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION**

**Who Can Sue:** "Any person aggrieved by a violation of this Act shall have a right of action in a State circuit court or as a supplemental claim in federal district court against an offending party." (Section 20(a)). [Source 1]

**Standing Requirements — Rosenbach v. Six Flags (2019 IL 123186):** In Rosenbach v. Six Flags Entertainment Corp. (2019 IL 123186), the Illinois Supreme Court held that a person need not sustain actual damages beyond a violation of their rights under BIPA in order to bring an action. The mere violation of the Act was sufficient to collect damages. The court ruled that users do not need to prove an injury (such as identity fraud or physical harm) in order to sue. [Source 3, Source 5, Source 22, Source 27]

This ruling led to a 1,400% increase in BIPA lawsuit filings, from 9 cases in 2018 to 134 in 2019, and 209 in 2020. Through September 2021, over 900 BIPA cases had been filed. [Source 19, Source 21, Source 27]

**PAGA-Style Claims:** BIPA does not contain a Private Attorneys General Act (PAGA)-style provision. There is no mechanism for private citizens to bring enforcement actions on behalf of the state. The private right of action is for individual or class-action claims only. [Source 1, Source 21]

**Class Action Dynamics:** 88% of BIPA lawsuits are employer-employee disputes from biometric timekeeping. 40% are filed against Illinois-based companies. In 8 consumer-oriented BIPA settlements, plaintiffs' lawyers received an average of $11.5 million per firm per case, while individuals received an average of $506 per case. [Source 19, Source 21]

**BIPA lacks procedural protections** such as notice and cure periods, safe harbors, damage caps, and exclusive AG enforcement — all recommended protections that other states have implemented. [Source 21]

**PART 5: TECHNOLOGY RESTRICTIONS**

**Definition of Biometric Identifiers:** "Biometric identifier means a retina or iris scan, fingerprint, voiceprint, or scan of hand or face geometry." (Section 10) [Source 1]

**What Is Excluded:** Writing samples, photographs, X-rays, medical images, and certain health information. [Source 1]

**Data Retention and Destruction Requirements:** A private entity in possession of biometric identifiers or biometric information must develop a written policy, made available to the public, establishing a retention schedule and guidelines for permanently destroying biometric identifiers and biometric information when the initial purpose for collecting or obtaining such identifiers or information has been satisfied or within 3 years of the individual's last interaction with the private entity, whichever occurs first. (Section 15(a)) [Source 1, Source 23]

**Prohibition on Selling Biometric Data:** "No private entity in possession of a biometric identifier or biometric information may sell, lease, trade, or otherwise profit from a person's or a customer's biometric identifier or biometric information." (Section 15(c)) [Source 1]

**Security Obligations:** Private entities must store and protect biometric data using reasonable industry standards. [Source 1, Source 3]

**PART 6: MAJOR ENFORCEMENT CASES**

**A. Rosenbach v. Six Flags Entertainment Corp. (2019 IL 123186)**

The Illinois Supreme Court ruled that a person need not have sustained actual damage beyond a violation of his or her rights under the Act in order to bring an action under it. This established that plaintiffs have standing based on mere procedural violations of BIPA, without any showing of actual injury. [Source 3, Source 5, Source 22]

**B. Cothron v. White Castle System, Inc. (2023 IL 128004)**

The Illinois Supreme Court, in a 4-3 decision, held that a separate claim accrues under the Act each time a private entity scans or transmits an individual's biometric identifier or information in violation of Section 15(b) or 15(d). The certified question from the Seventh Circuit was: "Do section 15(b) and 15(d) claims accrue each time a private entity scans a person's biometric identifier and each time a private entity transmits such a scan to a third party, respectively, or only upon the first scan and first transmission?" [Source 5, Source 15, Source 16, Source 17, Source 18]

The case involves Latrina Cothron, a White Castle employee since 2004, who filed a class action alleging that White Castle violated BIPA sections 15(b) and 15(d) by requiring employees to scan fingerprints to access pay stubs and computers without obtaining consent until 2018, a decade after the Act became effective in 2008. [Source 17]

**Key Reasoning from the Majority (Justice Rochford):**
- The plain language of Section 15(b) prohibits collecting, capturing, or obtaining biometric data without prior informed consent. The court found that "collect" and "capture" are not things that happen only once; each authentication scan constitutes a collection or capture because the system must capture the fingerprint each time for comparison.
- The "unless it first" phrase in Section 15(b) modifies the entity's obligation to obtain consent, not the triggering actions.
- Section 15(d) applies to every transmission to a third party. The terms "disclose" and "disseminate" are broad enough to include repeated transmissions to the same party.
- The court rejected White Castle's argument that injury occurs only upon initial loss of control, noting that Rosenbach established that the statutory violation itself is the injury.
- On the concern about potentially astronomical damages (White Castle estimated class-wide damages could exceed $17 billion for 9,500 employees), the court acknowledged the potential for significant awards but noted that damages are discretionary, not mandatory, under the Act, and suggested the legislature review these policy concerns. [Source 15, Source 17]

**Dissent (Justice Overstreet, joined by Chief Justice Theis and Justice Holder White):**
The dissent argued that the majority's interpretation "cannot be reconciled with the plain language of the statute," would lead to unintended consequences, and could "easily lead to annihilative liability for business." The dissent reasoned that the injury occurs only once—when biometric information is first obtained—as there is only "one loss of control or privacy." The dissent noted that in over 1,700 BIPA lawsuits since 2019, no plaintiff alleged a data breach or identity theft. Justice Overstreet argued that the majority's holding "subverted the intent of the Illinois General Assembly, threatens the survival of businesses in Illinois, and consequently raises significant constitutional due process concerns." The dissent noted that plaintiff Cothron alone could be entitled to over $7 million in damages for a single employee, despite no data breach or identity theft being alleged. [Source 14, Source 15, Source 16, Source 17]

The Illinois Supreme Court denied White Castle's petition for rehearing on July 18, 2023. [Source 14]

**Subsequent Legislative Fix:** The Illinois General Assembly responded with SB 2979, signed on August 2, 2024, which clarified that repeated collection of the same biometric identifier from the same person using the same method is a single violation allowing single recovery. [Source 12, Source 25, Source 28]

**C. Rogers v. BNSF Railway Co. (No. 1:19-cv-03083, N.D. Ill.)**

**Background:** This was the first BIPA case to go to trial in Illinois. On October 12, 2022, an Illinois jury ruled that BNSF Railway violated BIPA by scanning the fingerprints of 45,600 truck drivers without their written, informed consent when entering BNSF rail yards. The case involved BNSF's Auto-Gate System (AGS) at four Illinois railyards. BNSF contracted with Remprex (and previously Nascent) to install and manage the AGS. Remprex employees collected drivers' fingerprints (right thumb, left thumb, left index finger) without obtaining written consent or informing drivers of the specific purpose or retention period. [Source 5, Source 6, Source 7, Source 8, Source 9]

**Verdict:** The jury found that BNSF recklessly or intentionally committed 45,600 BIPA violations (one violation per class member), and the court entered a $228 million judgment (45,600 × $5,000 per violation). Lead plaintiff Richard Rogers said at a press conference after the verdict: "I'm really happy with the verdict today… all I ever wanted was justice for the over 45,000 truck drivers and myself." [Source 5, Source 6, Source 7, Source 8, Source 9]

**Vacatur and New Trial Order:** On June 30, 2023, U.S. District Judge Matthew Kennelly vacated the $228 million damages award and ordered a new trial limited to the question of damages. The court relied on the Illinois Supreme Court's decision in Cothron v. White Castle System, Inc., which noted that BIPA Section 20 uses the word "may" (discretionary) rather than "shall" (mandatory), meaning damages are discretionary, not mandatory. The court concluded that the amount of damages under BIPA Section 20 is discretionary and should be decided by the jury. [Source 7, Source 8, Source 9, Source 16]

**Settlement:** BNSF and the class ultimately reached a $75,000,000 settlement. The settlement website is bnsfbipaclassaction.com. The case is 2019-CH-04393. The court granted final approval on June 18, 2024, and payments were expected to mail on February 26, 2025. [Source 10]

**E. McDonald v. Symphony Bronzeville Park, LLC (2022 IL 126511)**

On February 3, 2022, the Illinois Supreme Court unanimously held that the Workers' Compensation Act's exclusivity provisions do not bar a claim for statutory damages under BIPA when an employer is alleged to have violated an employee's statutory privacy rights. Marquita McDonald filed a putative class action against her former employer, Bronzeville, alleging that the company collected, used, and stored employees' fingerprints in a biometric timekeeping system without providing required disclosures or obtaining written releases. [Source 5, Source 16, Source 22]

The court held that the key question is whether the injury "categorically fits within the purview of the Compensation Act." The court concluded that BIPA violations — which involve the loss of the ability to maintain privacy rights and the right to withhold consent — are fundamentally different in nature from the physical and psychological workplace injuries compensable under the Compensation Act. The court noted that the BIPA postdates the Compensation Act and specifically contemplates its application in the employment context by defining "written release" to include "a release executed by an employee as a condition of employment." [Source 16]

- **L.A. Tan Enterprises:** First BIPA settlement — $1.5 million (2016), with class members receiving $125–$150 each. [Source 3]
- **Biometric Impressions Corp.:** $10.85 million settlement (Sayas v. BioMetric Impressions Corp., Case No. 2020-CH-00210, Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois). Class period: January 8, 2015, to August 14, 2023. Payouts up to $480.52 as of June 2024. [Source 25]
- **Accu-Time Systems Inc.:** $1.5 million settlement (Franchini, et al. v. Accu-Time Systems, Inc., filed August 19, 2021). Covers approximately 12,000 individuals who scanned fingerprints at Accu-Time time clocks in Illinois between August 29, 2016, and September 15, 2025. Estimated payments between $100 and $500. Final approval hearing was April 1, 2026. [Source 21]
- **WorkEasy Software LLC (formerly EasyWorkforce):** $1.69 million settlement. Covers employees who used WorkEasy, EasyClocking, EasyWorkforce, or TimeLogix fingerprint time clocks in Illinois between June 24, 2016, and August 15, 2023. Approximately 21,915 individuals. Subclass members: $225–$750; other class members: $160–$500. Final approval granted April 28, 2026. An appeal was filed May 28, 2026, so payments are on hold. [Source 24]

**T. West Bend Mutual Ins. Co. v. Krishna Schaumburg Tan, Inc. (2021 IL 125978)**

In West Bend Mutual Ins. Co. v. Krishna Schaumburg Tan, Inc. (2021), the Illinois Supreme Court held that BIPA claims involve covered "publication" under general liability policies, and the violation of statutes exclusion (mentioning TCPA and CAN-SPAM Act but not BIPA) did not apply. [Source 5]

**Additional Cases Mentioned:**

- **Monroy v. Shutterfly, Inc.** — Facial recognition scanning of uploaded photos. [Source 3]
- **Rivera v. Google, Inc.** — Google Photos facial scans; dismissed for lack of standing. [Source 3]
- **Walton v. Roosevelt University (2023)** — Unionized employee claims may be preempted by the Labor Management Relations Act (LMRA). [Source 22]
- **Mosby v. Ingall Memorial Hospital** — Clarified that BIPA's healthcare exemptions apply to employees as well as patients. [Source 22]

---

**PART 7: ILLINOIS ATTORNEY GENERAL ENFORCEMENT ACTIONS**

The search results did not identify any specific BIPA enforcement actions brought by the Illinois Attorney General's office. The Illinois Attorney General is Kwame Raoul, who has been in office since 2019. [Source 14, Source 15]

The Office of the Attorney General's website lists its areas of focus as: Consumer Protection, Safer Communities, Preserving the Environment, Rights of the People, and Honest & Open Government. It provides tools for filing complaints (consumer fraud, civil rights, crime victim rights, disability rights, hate crimes, healthcare, workplace rights). [Source 14]

Notably, BIPA is a private right of action statute — it does not provide for exclusive enforcement by the Attorney General. The private right of action allows "any aggrieved person" to sue directly. [Source 1, Source 21]

The ILR Briefly report (October 2021) specifically notes that BIPA "lacks notice and cure periods, safe harbors, damage caps, and exclusive AG enforcement — all recommended protections." [Source 21]

---

**PART 8: ADDITIONAL CONTEXT**

**Litigation Statistics:**

- Between 2008-2016: Only 15 BIPA class actions filed. [Source 21]
- 2018: 9 cases. [Source 19]
- 2019: 134 cases (1,400% increase after Rosenbach). [Source 19]
- 2020: 209 cases. [Source 19]
- Through September 2021: Over 900 cases. [Source 21]
- By 2022-2023: Over 1,500 BIPA lawsuits. [Source 22]
- 88% of BIPA lawsuits are employer-employee disputes from biometric timekeeping. [Source 19, Source 21]
- 40% of BIPA cases are filed against Illinois-based companies. [Source 19]
- 78% of BIPA settlement cases involve workplace claims (employees); 22% involve non-workplace claims (customers). [Source 22]
- Median settlement per class member: $900 for workplace cases vs. $207 for non-workplace cases. [Source 22]
- Post-Cothron (February 2023), the share of workplace settlements above $1,000/class member rose from 34% to 46%, and the average workplace settlement increased from $838 to $1,049 per class member (a 25% increase). [Source 22]

**Other State Biometric Privacy Laws:**

Only two other states (Texas and Washington) have biometric privacy laws, and two cities (Washington DC and New York City) have active biometric privacy laws. However, none of these other laws provide a private right of action comparable to BIPA. [Source 5, Source 15, Source 27]

**Texas:** In July 2024, the Texas Attorney General secured a $1.4 billion settlement with Meta for alleged violations of Texas' biometric privacy law. [Source 29]

**Federal Legislation:** A proposed federal equivalent, the National Biometric Information Privacy Act of 2020 (S. 4400), was introduced by Senator Jeff Merkley but has not passed. [Source 3]

**Insurance Coverage Issues:**

Insurers are increasingly excluding BIPA claims from coverage. The West Bend Mutual case (2021) held that BIPA claims involve covered "publication" under general liability policies, but the article notes that "we're going to see more and more policies be very specific insofar as exclusions for biometric-related privacy information are concerned." [Source 5]

The 2026 Seventh Circuit ruling in Clay v. Union Pacific is expected to increase insurer-insured litigation over reasonableness of prior settlements, indemnity obligations, and recoupment of prior coverage payments. [Source 8, Source 26]

**Compliance Best Practices:**

A 5-step BIPA compliance roadmap has been identified:
1. Create and publish a written policy (include purpose, retention schedule — data must be destroyed within 3 years of last interaction, and destruction guidelines).
2. Get informed written consent BEFORE the first scan (electronic signatures are now valid).
3. Uphold reasonable care in data security.
4. Do not sell or profit from employee biometric data.
5. Manage vendors — businesses remain liable for third-party timeclock provider compliance. [Source 23]

**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

1. "Texas Business & Commerce Code § 503.001 biometric identifier act text"
2. "Texas CUBI Act 2025 2026 amendments"
3. "Texas Attorney General biometric enforcement actions"
4. "Texas CUBI vs Illinois BIPA comparison private right of action"
5. "Texas HB 4705 Biometric Data Privacy Act 2023 passed or failed"
6. "Texas TRAIGA amendments to CUBI biometric identifier act 2025"
7. "Texas Attorney General Google biometric settlement 2024 2025"
8. "Texas common law privacy claim biometric data intrusion upon seclusion"
9. "Texas biometric enforcement actions 2023 2024 2025 2026 settlements"
10. "Texas TRAIGA Act amendments CUBI biometric identifier 2025"
11. "Texas 89th Legislature 2025 biometric identifier bill amendment CUBI"
12. "Texas Attorney General biometric enforcement action 2023 2024 2025 other company"
13. "Texas Business Commerce Code 503.001 current 2026 codified"
14. "Texas Business Commerce Code 503.001 2025 version AI exemption"
15. "Texas Business Commerce Code 503.001 2025 amendments TRAIGA"

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

**1. Enactment Date and Amendments through 2026**

The Texas Capture or Use of Biometric Identifier Act (CUBI) was originally enacted in 2001 and recodified in 2009 at Texas Business & Commerce Code § 503.001 [1][17][35]. CUBI was signed into law by then-Governor Rick Perry in 2009, making Texas one of the first three U.S. states (along with Illinois and Washington) to regulate biometric data for commercial purposes [7][35]. The statute was amended in 2009, 2017 [46], and most significantly in 2025 by the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (TRAIGA), House Bill 149 [7][8][31].

**The TRAIGA Amendments (HB 149) – Effective January 1, 2026:**

TRAIGA was signed by Governor Greg Abbott on June 22, 2025, and takes effect January 1, 2026 [7][8][31][38]. The law amends CUBI in several critical ways:

- **AI Model Training Exemption:** The current statute (as reflected in the FindLaw codification) now exempts "the training, processing, or storage of biometric identifiers involved in developing, training, evaluating, disseminating, or otherwise offering artificial intelligence models or systems, unless a system is used or deployed for the purpose of uniquely identifying a specific individual" [1]. This exemption was added by TRAIGA [31][34][50].

- **Security and Fraud Prevention Exemption:** Also exempted is "developing or deploying an artificial intelligence system for the purpose of security, fraud prevention, system integrity, or investigating illegal activities" [1][50].

- **Subsequent Commercial Use Trap:** If a biometric identifier captured for AI training is later used for a commercial purpose not covered by the exemptions, the possessor becomes subject to the possession/destruction requirements and penalties of CUBI [1][31].

- **Publicly Available Content Does Not Equal Consent:** TRAIGA clarifies that consent is not implied merely by the existence of an image or media on the internet or public sources, "unless the individual themselves made it public" [1][31][32][34].

**HB 4705 (2023) – Biometric Data Privacy Act of 2023 – Did Not Pass:**

HB 4705 was introduced in the 88th Legislature Regular Session on March 10, 2023, by Representative Briscoe Cain [4][20]. It proposed to significantly expand CUBI by:
- Adding a definition of "biometric information" beyond "biometric identifier"
- Adding additional identifiers (palm or vascular vein patterns, heartbeat, keystrokes, signature, gait)
- Requiring **written** notice and a **written release** (signed consent) before capture
- Adding a **private right of action** allowing affected individuals to sue
- The bill was referred to the Business & Industry Committee on March 22, 2023, and **died on May 29, 2023** (end of session) [4][20].

**Senate Bill 2490 (2025) – Referred but Status Unclear:**
SB 2490, a companion to HB 3755, was referred to the Senate Business and Commerce Committee on April 3, 2025. The bill proposed amending CUBI to exempt AI-related activities from §503.001 unless the biometric identifier is used to uniquely identify a specific individual [47]. This appears to overlap with the TRAIGA amendments that ultimately passed.

**No Other 2025-2026 Amendments:**
According to the Holland & Knight 2026 legal alert, the Texas legislature will not be in regular session again until 2027 ["New privacy legislation is unlikely unless the Texas governor calls a special session and the topic is addressed during that session"] [7].

---

**2. Consent Mechanisms: Notice and Consent Requirements**

Under current CUBI, a person may not capture a biometric identifier of an individual for a commercial purpose unless the person: "(1) informs the individual before capturing the biometric identifier; and (2) receives the individual's consent to capture the biometric identifier" [1][3][45][46].

Key aspects of the consent requirement:

- **Opt-In Regime:** CUBI requires affirmative consent – it is an opt-in framework, not opt-out [3][35].
- **No Written Release Required:** Unlike Illinois BIPA (which requires "a written release executed by the individual"), CUBI does not explicitly require written consent; it only requires that the individual be informed and consent be received [1][15][16]. However, businesses are advised to obtain written or electronic consent records for auditability [3][50].
- **Consent Cannot Be Implied from Public Availability:** The statute as amended by TRAIGA clarifies that consent is not implied merely by the existence of an image or media on the internet or public sources, unless the individual themselves made it public [1][31][32].
- **Notice Must Be Given Before Capture:** The statute requires informing the individual *before* capturing the biometric identifier [1][3]. Consent collected after the first scan is a violation [50].
- **Commercial Purpose Requirement:** CUBI only applies when biometric identifiers are captured for a "commercial purpose." The term "commercial purpose" is not defined in the statute but **Texas courts have defined it as purposes "intended to result in a profit or other tangible benefit"** [122][44]. The Texas AG has taken the position that improving AI models alone qualifies as a commercial purpose [12].

**Key Differences from Illinois BIPA:**

| Aspect | Texas CUBI | Illinois BIPA |
|---------|-------------|----------------|
| Consent Type | Inform + receive consent | Written notice + written release (signed) |
| Notice | Before capture | Before collection (written, specific purpose and retention term) |
| Retention Policy | No explicit written policy requirement | Must maintain and publicly disclose written retention/destruction policy |
| Private Right of Action | No (only AG) | Yes (any aggrieved person) |
| Statute of Limitations | Likely 2 years (trespass to personal rights) | 5 years (Tims v. Black Horse) |
| Maximum Retention | 1 year after purpose expires | 3 years after last interaction |

[15][16][17][18]

---

**3. Penalty Structure**

**Statutory Damages:** CUBI imposes a civil penalty of **not more than $25,000 per violation** [1][10][14][45][46]. There is **no statutory minimum** and **no cap** on total penalties [14][35][44]. The Texas Attorney General can aggregate violationsacross millions of individuals, leading to massive potential exposure [12][14][50].

**Double Counting of Violations:** The Texas Attorney General has argued that **both the collection of a biometric identifier without consent AND the subsequent storage of that identifier constitute separate violations**, potentially doubling the penalty to $50,000 per instance [12][14]. In the Meta complaint, the AG alleged this theory: "Because Facebook's possession of biometric identifiers in the first instance was unlawful, maintaining possession of these biometric identifiers for any period of time is unreasonable, and violates [CUBI]" [12].

**Enforcement Mechanism:** Only the Texas Attorney General may bring an action to recover civil penalties. The statute provides: "The attorney general may bring an action to recover the civil penalty" [1][5][45]. There is **no private right of action** under CUBI [10][15][16][17][44].

**Other Available Remedies:** In addition to civil penalties, the AG can seek **injuctive relief** [12][28]. The AG may also bring claims under the **Texas Deceptive Trade Practices-Consumer Protection Act (DTPA)** alongside CUBI claims, as was done in the Meta and Google cases [10][13][21]. Penalties under the DTPA can include additional civil penalties of up to $20,000 per violation.

**TRAIGA Penalties (Separate but Related):** The TRAIGA (effective Jan 1, 2026) imposes its own penalty structure for AI-related violations, including: $10,000-$12,000 per curable violation; $80,000-$200,000 per uncurable violation; and $2,000-$40,000 per day for continuing violations [31][32][33][48]. State agencies may impose additional sanctions including up to $100,000 fines and license suspension/revocation [31][48]. There is a 60-day cure period before AG enforcement [31][33][48].

**Texas Data Privacy and Security Act (TDPSA) Penalties:** The TDPSA (effective July 1, 2024) allows the AG to levy civil penalties of up to $7,500 per violation [20][43]. Unlike CUBI, the TDPSA treats biometric data as "sensitive data" but does not provide its own private right of action [7][20].

---

**4. Private Right of Action**

**CUBI Does NOT Provide a Private Right of Action:** It is well established that CUBI is enforceable only by the Texas Attorney General [1][5][10][15][16][17][44][45][46]. The statutory text states only "The attorney general may bring an action to recover the civil penalty" [1]. This is the most significant difference between Texas CUBI and Illinois BIPA [16][18].

**HB 4705 (2023) Would Have Added One But Died:** HB 4705 proposed to amend the statute to state: "The attorney general, or an individual affected by a violation of this section, may bring an action to recover the civil penalty" [4]. The bill died in committee on May 29, 2023 [20].

**Developents in Texas Courts Regarding Common Law Privacy Claims or Other Statutes That Could Be Used:**

While CUBI has no private right of action, Texas recognizes several common law privacy torts that could potentially be used by individuals alleging biometric privacy violations:

**a. Inrusion on Seclision:** Texas recognizes the tort of intrusion on seclusion [16][25]. The elements are: (1) the defendant intentionally invaded the plaintiff's private matters without authorization; (2) the invasion is offensive to a reasonable person; (3) the matter intruded upon is private; and (4) the intrusion caused mental anguish or suffering [19]. The intrusion itself is actionable regardless of whether information is communicated to others [19]. Texas courts have recognized this tort in cases involving electronic surveillance and unauthorized access to private information [16][25].

**b. Misappropriation of Name or Likeness:** Texas recognizes the tort of misappropriation (unauthorized use of a person's name or likeness for commercial purposes) [16][25].

**c. Public Disclosure of Private Facts:** Texas recognizes the tort of public disclosure of private facts, which could apply to unauthorized disclosure of biometric data [16][25].

**d. Texas Does NOT Recognize False Light:** Texas has expressly refused to adopt a claim for false light invasion of privacy, finding it substantially duplicates defamation [16][25].

**e. Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act (DTPA):** While individuals can bring DTPA claims for false, misleading, or deceptive acts, the Texas AG has used the DTPA alongside CUBI in its own enforcement actions [10][13][21]. It is unclear whether an individual could successfully bring a DTPA claim based solely on biometric data collection without additional misleading conduct.

**f. Statute of Limitations:** The applicable statute of limitations for privacy torts in Texas is 2 years (trespass to personal rights) [16][25].

**g. Practical Consideration:** Because CUBI has no private right of action, no class actions have been filed under CUBI [50]. This contrasts sharply with Illinois, where BIPA has generated over 900 class actions through 2021 alone [18] and at least messages.content:
Here are the cleaned, comprehensive findings from the research conducted on the Washington State Biometric Privacy Law (HB 1493 / RCW 19.375).

---

**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

1.  Search: "Washington State biometric privacy law RCW 19.375 HB 1493"
2.  Search: "RCW 19.375 Washington biometric privacy statute full text"
3.  Search: "Washington HB 1493 biometric privacy 2017 amendments 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026"
4.  Search: "Washington HB 1493 biometric privacy amendments 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 legislative history"
5.  Search: "Washington My Health My Data Act biometric privacy interaction"
6.  Search: "Washington biometric privacy law court cases enforcement AG attorney general"
7.  Search: "Washington State facial recognition law 2020 2021 2022 2023"
8.  Search: "Washington RCW 19.375 amended 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 bill history"
9.  Search: "Washington Consumer Protection Act biometric private right of action RCW 19.375.030"
10. Search: "Washington biometric privacy lawsuit class action enforcement AG attorney general"
11. Search: "Washington My Health My Data Act RCW 19.375 biometric interaction comparison"
12. Search: "Washington biometric privacy law RCW 19.375 no amendments unchanged 2017 2026"
13. Search: "Washington Consumer Protection Act private right of action biometric violation RCW 19.375.030"
14. Search: "Washington Attorney General biometric privacy enforcement action HB 1493"
15. Search: "Washington biometric privacy class action lawsuit court case 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025"

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

**1. Enactment Date and Legislative History**

- **Enactment:** On May 16, 2017, Washington Governor Jay Inslee signed House Bill 1493 (H.B. 1493) into law, making Washington the third U.S. state (after Illinois and Texas) to enact biometric privacy legislation. [Hunter, 2017] [Inside Privacy, 2017]
- **Effective Date:** The law became effective on July 23, 2017. [Hunter, 2017] [Inside Privacy, 2017]
- **Codification:** The law is codified at Chapter 19.375 RCW (Revised Code of Washington), sections 19.375.010 through 19.375.900. [WA Legislature, RCW 19.375]
- **Companion Bill:** On the same day, Governor Inslee also signed H.B. 1717, which covers the collection and use of biometric identifiers by state government agencies. [WaTech, 2017] [Inside Privacy, 2017]
- **Amendments (2017-2026):** Based on available research, **no amendments to RCW 19.375 have been identified through the 2026 legislative sessions.** The statute text available on the official Washington State Legislature website (app.leg.wa.gov) and on Justia (2025 edition) shows the statute was enacted by "2017 c 299 s 2-4" and does not reflect any subsequent amendments. [Justia, 2025] [WA Legislature, RCW 19.375]
- **Legislative Intent:** The legislature found that "citizens of Washington are increasingly asked to disclose sensitive biological information that uniquely identifies them for commerce, security, and convenience. The collection and marketing of biometric information about individuals, without consent or knowledge of the individual whose data is collected, is of increasing concern." [RCW 19.375.900] [WA Legislature, RCW 19.375]

**2. Consent Mechanisms**

- **General Prohibition:** A person may not enroll a biometric identifier in a database for a commercial purpose without first providing notice, obtaining consent, or providing a mechanism to prevent the subsequent use of a biometric identifier for a commercial purpose. [RCW 19.375.020(1)]
- **Definition of Notice:** Notice is a disclosure, that is not considered affirmative consent, that is given through a procedure reasonably designed to be readily available to affected individuals. [RCW 19.375.020(2)]
- **Consent Standard:** The exact type of notice and consent required is "context-dependent." The law does not specify the exact type of notice required. [Inside Privacy, 2017]
- **No Written Consent Requirement:** Unlike Illinois' BIPA, which requires written notice and release before collection, Washington's law does not require written consent. [TermsFeed, 2017]
- **Opt-In vs. Opt-Out:** The statute requires a form of opt-in consent for enrollment of biometric identifiers for a commercial purpose. The law provides that a person must provide "notice, obtaining consent, or providing a mechanism to prevent the subsequent use of a biometric identifier for a commercial purpose" — the third option (providing a mechanism to prevent subsequent use) is functionally an opt-out mechanism for subsequent commercial use, but the initial enrollment still requires notice and consent. [RCW 19.375.020]
- **Material Changes:** A person who enrolls or obtains a biometric identifier for commercial purposes may not **use or disclose** it in a manner materially inconsistent with the original terms without obtaining consent for the new terms. [RCW 19.375.020(5)]
- **Security Purpose Exception:** Nothing in the section requires an entity to provide notice and obtain consent to collect, capture, or enroll a biometric identifier and store it in a biometric system, or otherwise, in furtherance of a security purpose. [RCW 19.375.020(7)]

**3. Penalty Structure**

- **Key Correction:** The user's prompt mentioned "statutory damages of $5,000 per violation." This figure is from **Illinois' Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA)**, which provides $1,000 for negligent violations and $5,000 for intentional/reckless violations. **Washington's law does NOT have statutory damages.** [Squire Patton Boggs, 2025] [EBGLaw, 2024]
- **Enforcement Under CPA:** A violation of RCW 19.375 is considered an unfair or deceptive act in trade or commerce and an unfair method of competition for the purpose of applying the Washington Consumer Protection Act (CPA), Chapter 19.86 RCW. [RCW 19.375.030(1)]
- **CPA Penalties:** The Attorney General can obtain civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation, and enhanced penalties of $5,000 if the unlawful acts or practices targeted or impacted certain protected classes. [Multilaw/Miller Nash, 2025]
- **AG Enforcement:** The CPA allows the Attorney General to seek injunctions, civil penalties, and legal fees. [CaseGuard, 2017] [Multilaw/Miller Nash, 2025]
- **Actual Damages:** Under the CPA, private plaintiffs (if they could bring a claim — see Section 4) would need to prove actual damages. [Steptoe, 2024]
- **Treble Damages (CPA):** The CPA allows for treble damages up to $25,000, plus costs and attorneys' fees, for private actions under the CPA. [Steptoe, 2024] [Multilaw/Miller Nash, 2025]
- **My Health My Data Act Penalties:** Under the MHMDA, the Washington AG can impose civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation ($12,500 if targeting vulnerable populations). [Steptoe, 2024]

**4. Private Right of Action**

- **RCW 19.375 — No Private Right of Action:** The statute explicitly states: "This chapter may be enforced solely by the attorney general under the consumer protection act, chapter 19.86 RCW." [RCW 19.375.030(2)] [Justia, 2025]
- **Consistent Interpretation:** All sources agree that RCW 19.375 does not create a private right of action for individuals. Only the Washington Attorney General can enforce the law. [Hunter, 2017] [Inside Privacy, 2017] [FKKS, 2017] [DWT, 2017] [Eisenhower Carlson, 2017] [TermsFeed, 2017] [Hyperproof, 2017]
- **Key Distinction from Illinois:** This is a critical difference from Illinois' BIPA, which allows private lawsuits and has generated significant class action litigation (e.g., $650M Facebook settlement, $36M Six Flags settlement). [Hunter, 2017] [DWT, 2017] [Debevoise, 2021]
- **CPA Private Right of Action Tension:** While some sources note that the CPA generally provides a private right of action, RCW 19.375.030(2) explicitly limits enforcement "solely by the attorney general." This means that while violations are deemed CPA violations, only the AG can bring an enforcement action under this specific chapter. The statute is clear that there is no private right of action for biometric violations under RCW 19.375. [RCW 19.375.030] [Justia, 2025]
- **My Health My Data Act — Private Right of Action:** The Washington My Health My Data Act (MHMDA), effective March 31, 2024, provides a private right of action for violations of its provisions. Biometric data is included in MHMDA's definition of "consumer health data." Under MHMDA, private plaintiffs must prove actual damages (no statutory damages like BIPA), and courts have discretion to treble damages up to a $25,000 cap, plus costs and attorneys' fees. [Steptoe, 2024] [Hintze Law, 2023] [Goodwin, 2023]
- **Washington Supreme Court / Appellate Cases:** No Washington Supreme Court decisions or appellate cases specifically interpreting RCW 19.375 were found in the search results. The statute has not generated significant litigation compared to Illinois' BIPA. [Squire Patton Boggs, 2025]

**5. Technology Restrictions**

- **Definition of Biometric Identifier (RCW 19.375.010):** "Data generated by automatic measurements of an individual's biological characteristics, such as a fingerprint, voiceprint, eye retinas, irises, or other unique biological patterns or characteristics that is used to identify a specific individual." [RCW 19.375.010] [Justia, 2025]
- **Exclusions from Definition (RCW 19.375.010):** The definition does NOT include: (a) a physical or digital photograph, video or audio recording or data generated therefrom; or (b) information collected, used, or stored for health care treatment, payment, or operations under HIPAA. [RCW 19.375.010] [Justia, 2025]
- **Facial Recognition Exclusion:** The exclusion of photographs, video, and audio recordings "suggests the statute will have limited application in the context of facial recognition technology." [Inside Privacy, 2017] [Hunter, 2017]
- **Gait and Keystroke Patterns:** These are NOT explicitly listed in RCW 19.375's definition of "biometric identifier." However, the statute's definition includes "other unique biological patterns or characteristics," which could be interpreted broadly. [RCW 19.375.010]
- **Definition of Enroll (RCW 19.375.010):** "To capture a biometric identifier of an individual, convert it into a reference template that cannot be reconstructed into the original output image, and store it in a database that matches the biometric identifier to a specific individual." [RCW 19.375.010] [Justia, 2025]
- **Definition of Commercial Purpose (RCW 19.375.010):** "A purpose in furtherance of the sale or disclosure to a third party of a biometric identifier for the purpose of marketing of goods or services when such goods or services are unrelated to the initial transaction in which a person first gains possession of an individual's biometric identifier." This does NOT include a security or law enforcement purpose. [RCW 19.375.010] [Justia, 2025]
- **Definition of Security Purpose (RCW 19.375.010):** Prevents shoplifting, fraud, theft, and protects the security or integrity of software, accounts, applications, online services, or any person. [RCW 19.375.010] [Justia, 2025]
- **Data Retention Requirements (RCW 19.375.020(4)):** A person who knowingly possesses a biometric identifier enrolled for a commercial purpose may retain the biometric identifier no longer than is reasonably necessary to: (a) comply with a court order or statute; (b) protect against fraud, criminal activity, or security threats; or (c) provide the services for which the biometric identifier was enrolled. [RCW 19.375.020(4)] [WA Legislature, RCW 19.375]
- **Note on Retention:** Some secondary sources state the law requires biometric data be destroyed within a reasonable time after it has served its purpose or within three years of the individual's last interaction, whichever is earlier. [Hyperproof, 2017] However, this three-year provision is not explicitly stated in the statutory text of RCW 19.375.020; the statute uses the "reasonably necessary" standard.
- **Data Security Requirements (RCW 19.375.020(4)):** Must take reasonable care to guard against unauthorized access to and acquisition of biometric identifiers. [RCW 19.375.020(4)]
- **Prohibition on Selling Biometric Data:** Unless consent has been obtained, a person who has enrolled an individual's biometric identifier may not sell, lease, or otherwise disclose the biometric identifier to another person for a commercial purpose, except in specific circumstances. [RCW 19.375.020(3)]
- **Exceptions to Sale/Disclosure Prohibition:** Disclosure is permitted if: (a) consistent with the section's requirements; (b) necessary to provide a requested product or service; (c) necessary to complete a financial transaction; (d) required or expressly authorized by law or court order; (e) made to a third party contractually bound to protect the identifier; or (f) made to prepare for litigation or participate in judicial process. [RCW 19.375.020(3)]
- **Unenrolled Biometric Identifiers:** The limitations on disclosure and retention do not apply to unenrolled biometric identifiers. [RCW 19.375.020(6)]
- **Scope of Regulation:** Washington's statute is limited to persons who "enroll" biometric identifiers, rather than broadly regulating the capture or possession of biometric data. [Hunter, 2017]
- **Exclusions (RCW 19.375.040):** The law does not apply to: (a) financial institutions subject to the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act; (b) activities subject to HIPAA; or (c) law enforcement officers acting within their authority. [WA Legislature, RCW 19.375]
- **Separate Facial Recognition Law (SB 6280):** In March 2020, Washington passed SB 6280, the first law in the U.S. expressly regulating government use of facial recognition technology, effective July 2021. It applies to state and local government agencies and their vendors. It requires accountability reports, meaningful human review for decisions with legal effects, and independent testing for accuracy and fairness. It has no private right of action and no penalty/enforcement mechanism, and was criticized by the ACLU as having "no teeth." [Knobbe Martens, 2021] [Butzel Long, 2020] [Honigman, 2020]

**6. Enforcement Cases**

- **No RCW 19.373-Specific AG Enforcement Actions Found:** No specific Washington Attorney General enforcement actions under RCW 19.375 (HB 1493) were identified in the search results.
- **No RCW 19.375 Class Actions Found:** Because the statute does not provide a private right of action, there are no class action lawsuits under RCW 19.375 itself. [Hunter, 2017] [DWT, 2017] [TermsFeed, 2017]
- **First MHMDA Lawsuit — Maxwell v. Amazon.com, Inc. (Feb 10, 2025):** The first class action complaint was filed under the My Health My Data Act, alleging Amazon collected consumer health data (including biometric data and precise location) through its SDKs in mobile apps without proper consent or disclosures. The defendant's response deadline was April 21, 2025. [Orrick, 2025] [Paul Hastings, 2025]
- **Clearview AI Settlement (March 2025):** A federal judge approved a $51.75 million settlement in the Clearview AI biometric privacy multidistrict litigation. The settlement was unusual — rather than cash, the class received a 23% equity stake in Clearview AI. [Regulatory Oversight, 2025] [Squire Patton Boggs, 2025]
- **Texas AG v. Meta (2024):** Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton secured a $1.4 billion settlement with Meta (Facebook) over its unauthorized capture and use of personal biometric data from millions of Texans. This was the first lawsuit and settlement under Texas's Capture or Use of Biometric Identifier Act (CUBI). [Texas AG, 2024]
- **Texas AG v. Google (2025):** Texas entered into a $1.375 billion settlement with Google, including for alleged violations of CUBI. [Squire Patton Boggs, 2025]
- **Illinois BIPA Litigation (for context):** BIPA has generated massive litigation: Facebook settled for $650M (2020), TikTok for $92M (2021), Google for $100M (2022). The *Rosenbach v. Six Flags* (Illinois Supreme Court, 2019) decision held plaintiffs need not prove actual injury. The *Cothron v. White Castle* (Illinois Supreme Court, 2023) decision held each scan counts as a separate violation, exposing White Castle to potential $17B in liability. BNSF Railway faced a $228M jury verdict. In August 2024, Illinois amended BIPA to limit damages to one violation per person for notice-and-consent claims. [EBGLaw, 2024] [Gen Re, 2024] [Squire Patton Boggs, 2025]
- **BIPA 2025 Activity:** At least 100 putative BIPA class actions were filed in 2025. [Squire Patton Boggs, 2025]

**7. Comparison with Washington My Health My Data Act (MHMDA) and Other State Privacy Laws**

- **MHMDA Enactment:** Signed into law on April 27, 2023, effective March 31, 2024 (June 30, 2024 for small businesses). [Goodwin, 2023] [FPF, 2023]
- **MHMDA Motivation:** Motivated partly by the *Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization* Supreme Court decision to protect reproductive health data. [FPF, 2023] [Goodwin, 2024]
- **MHMDA Codification:** RCW § 19.373. [Multilaw/Miller Nash, 2025]
- **Broader Definition of Biometric Data:** MHMDA defines biometric data much more broadly than RCW 19.375. It includes "data generated from the measurement or technological processing of an individual's physiological, biological, or behavioral characteristics and that identifies a consumer, whether individually or in combination with other data." It explicitly includes: imagery of iris, retina, fingerprint, face, hand, palm, vein patterns, voice recordings, keystroke patterns or rhythms, and gait patterns or rhythms. Unlike RCW 19.375, it does NOT exclude photographs, videos, or audio recordings. [Hintze Law, 2023] [Goodwin, 2023] [BCLP/JDSupra, 2023] [Quarles, 2023]
- **MHMDA — Data That "Could" Identify:** Under MHMDA, data that "can be" used to extract a biometric template is sufficient — actual extraction is not required. [Quarles, 2023]
- **MHMDA — Employee/B2B Exclusion:** MHMDA excludes employee data and B2B data, unlike RCW 19.375 and Illinois BIPA, which apply to workplace contexts. [Hintze Law, 2023] [Quarles, 2023]
- **MHMDA — Consent Standard:** Requires a GDPR-level of consent — "a clear affirmative act" — for collection and sharing of consumer health data, but only for secondary purposes (not for primary collection necessary to provide a requested product/service). [Hintze Law, 2023] [FPF, 2023]
- **MHMDA — Private Right of Action:** MHMDA provides a private right of action through the Washington CPA. Violations are treated as unfair or deceptive trade practices. Private plaintiffs must prove actual damages, with courts having discretion to award treble damages up to $25,000. This makes Washington the second state (after Illinois) to provide a private right of action for biometric data privacy claims. [Steptoe, 2024] [Hintze Law, 2023] [Goodwin, 2023]
- **MHMDA — Consumer Rights:** Grants rights to confirm processing, access health data, delete health data, withdraw consent, and access lists of third parties with whom data was shared or sold. [FPF, 2023] [Goodwin, 2024]
- **MHMDA — Geofencing Prohibition:** Forbids geofencing (virtual boundary of 2,000 feet or less) around healthcare facilities to identify/track consumers, collect health data, or send health-related notifications/advertisements. [FPF, 2023] [Goodwin, 2024]
- **MHMDA — No Retention Limitation:** Unlike RCW 19.375, MHMDA does not have a data retention limitation. [Hintze Law, 2023]
- **Overlap and Interaction:** "A great deal of biometric data will be subject to both Washington laws." [Hintze Law, 2023] Compliance with RCW 19.375 does not guarantee compliance with MHMDA, and vice versa. [Quarles, 2023]
- **Security Purpose Exclusions in Both Laws:** Both MHMDA and RCW 19.375 have exclusions that apply to security-related uses of biometric data, meaning many common biometric use cases (e.g., workplace time clocks, device unlocking) may be exempt from MHMDA's substantive compliance requirements. [Hintze Law, 2023]
- **Comparison with Illinois BIPA:** Washington's RCW 19.375 is considered "much weaker" than Illinois' BIPA because it: (1) has no private right of action; (2) excludes photographs, video, and audio recordings; (3) only applies to "enrolled" identifiers; (4) provides a safe harbor for security purposes; (5) does not require written consent; and (6) has a narrower definition of commercial purpose. [TermsFeed, 2017] [DWT, 2017]
- **Comparison with Texas CUBI:** Washington's law is similar to Texas in that both are enforced only by the Attorney General, unlike Illinois which has a private right of action. [Inside Privacy, 2017] [Hunter, 2017]
- **Current Status (2026):** Washington remains one of only three states (Illinois, Texas, Washington) with a standalone biometric privacy statute, though other states have introduced biometric privacy bills. [BCLP, 2026]
- **Proposed Legislation — Washington People's Privacy Act (HB 1671):** A February 2025 testimony from EPIC supported HB 1671, which would provide comprehensive privacy protections including data minimization, strong protections for sensitive data (including biometrics), and a private right of action under the CPA. [EPIC, 2025]
- **Washington Constitution:** The Washington Constitution explicitly recognizes privacy as a fundamental right. [Multilaw/Miller Nash, 2025]
- **CPA Generally:** The CPA prohibits unfair or deceptive acts in trade/commerce. It provides both AG enforcement and a private right of action (though the biometric chapter limits enforcement to the AG). CPA private actions can recover treble damages up to $25,000 plus costs and attorneys' fees. [Multilaw/Miller Nash, 2025]

---

**Key Corrections to User's Prompt Assumptions**

1. **$5,000 Statutory Damages:** This is from Illinois' BIPA (for intentional/reckless violations), NOT Washington's law. Washington's RCW 19.375 does not have statutory damages. [Squire Patton Boggs, 2025]
2. **Private Right of Action:** RCW 19.375 does NOT provide a private right of action — enforcement is solely by the Attorney General. However, the My Health My Data Act (2023) DOES provide a private right of action for biometric data classified as consumer health data. [RCW 19.375.030] [Steptoe, 2024]
3. **Gait and Keystroke Patterns:** These are NOT explicitly listed in RCW 19.375's definition of biometric identifiers. They ARE included in the MHMDA's broader definition. [RCW 19.375.010] [BCLP/JDSupra, 2023]
4. **Facial Recognition:** RCW 19.375 explicitly excludes photographs, video, and audio recordings, so it has limited application to facial recognition technology. Separate facial recognition regulation exists under SB 6280 for government use. [Inside Privacy, 2017] [Knobbe Martens, 2021]
5. **No Amendments Found:** RCW 19.375 has not been amended since its 2017 enactment, based on available legislative records. [Justia, 2025] [WA Legislature, RCW 19.375]

---

**List of All Relevant Sources (with citations in the report)**

[1] *Washington State Legislature, Chapter 19.375 RCW: Biometric Identifiers*: https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=19.375&full=true

[2] *Washington State Legislature, RCW 19.375.020: Enrollment, disclosure, and retention of biometric identifiers*: https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=19.375.020

[3] *Justia, 2025 Revised Code of Washington, Title 19, Chapter 19.375, Section 19.375.010 - Definitions*: https://law.justia.com/codes/washington/title-19/chapter-19-375/section-19-375-010

[4] *Justia, 2025 Revised Code of Washington, Title 19, Chapter 19.375, Section 19.375.020 - Enrollment, disclosure, and retention*: https://law.justia.com/codes/washington/title-19/chapter-19-375/section-19-375-020

[5] *Justia, 2025 Revised Code of Washington, Title 19, Chapter 19.375, Section 19.375.030 - Application of consumer protection act*: https://law.justia.com/codes/washington/title-19/chapter-19-375/section-19-375-030

[6] *Hunter, 2017, Hunton & Williams, "Washington Becomes Third State to Enact Biometric Privacy Law"*: https://www.hunton.com/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/washington-becomes-third-state-enact-biometric-privacy-law

**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

1. Search for: "740 ILCS 14/1-99 Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act text current 2026"
2. Search for: "Illinois BIPA 2024 amendment per-scan damages"
3. Search for: "Illinois BIPA 2025 2026 amendments legislative update"
4. Search for: "Cothron v. White Castle 2023 Illinois Supreme Court per-scan BIPA"
5. Search for: "BIPA class action settlement Target Macy's Lowe's Home Depot Walgreens case number docket"
6. Search for: "BNSF Railway BIPA class action $228 million verdict Rogers case number"
7. Search for: "Vance v. Amazon BIPA class action settlement"
8. Search for: "Schanowitz v. State Farm BIPA case"
9. Search for: "Illinois Attorney General BIPA enforcement action"
10. Search for: "BIPA 2025 2026 amendment legislative update Illinois"
11. Search for: "Macy's BIPA class action lawsuit biometric fingerprint Illinois"
12. Search for: "Lowe's Home Depot BIPA biometric class action lawsuit Illinois"
13. Search for: "Illinois Attorney General BIPA enforcement action Kwame Raoul"
14. Search for: "McDonald v. Symphony Bronzeville Park BIPA Illinois Supreme Court 2022"
15. Search for: "BIPA hospital employee time clock fingerprint class action lawsuit"
16. Search for: "Facebook BIPA $650 million settlement In re Facebook biometric privacy"
17. Search for: "Clearview AI BIPA Illinois settlement class action"

---

**FULLY COMPREHENSIVE FINDINGS**

**PART 1: THE STATUTE — ILLINOIS BIOMETRIC INFORMATION PRIVACY ACT (740 ILCS 14/1-99)**

**Enactment and Legislative History**

The Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) is codified at 740 ILCS 14/1-99. It was enacted on October 3, 2008 (P.A. 95-994), effective immediately, after being introduced by Senator Terry Link on February 14, 2008 (SB 2400), and passing both houses unanimously (113-0 House, 42-0 Senate), and signed by Governor Rod Blagojevich. [Source 1, Source 3, Source 28]

BIPA is considered the most stringent biometric privacy law in the U.S. (compared to Texas and Washington, which have similar but weaker protections). It was the first U.S. law to regulate private-sector use of biometric identifiers. [Source 3, Source 22]

**Amendments**

- **August 2, 2024 Amendment (SB 2979 / P.A. 103-769):** Signed into law by Governor J.B. Pritzker, effective immediately. This amendment made two key changes: (1) It limits damages by providing that a private entity that collects or discloses biometric data from the same person using the same method in more than one instance commits a single violation, entitling the aggrieved person to at most one recovery. (2) It updates the definition of "written release" to include electronic signatures, defined as "an electronic sound, symbol, or process attached to or logically associated with a record and executed or adopted by a person with the intent to sign the record." This confirmed that checkboxes or other electronic confirmations are sufficient. [Source 1, Source 2, Source 12, Source 25, Source 28]

- **2025-2026 Amendments:** No additional amendments beyond the 2024 amendment have been identified as of the current date (August 23, 2026). The 2024 amendment remains the most recent legislative change. [Source 1, Source 2, Source 22]

**Key Statutory Provisions**

**Section 5 — Legislative Findings:** The General Assembly's findings (Section 5) emphasize ties to finances and personal information, and locations like grocery stores and gas stations, implying a minimum level of known contact. [Source 4]

**Section 10 — Definitions:** "Biometric identifiers" include a retina or iris scan, fingerprint, voiceprint, or scan of hand or face geometry. Excluded from the definition are: writing samples, photographs, X-rays, medical images, and certain health information. "Private entity" means any individual, partnership, corporation, LLC, etc., but excludes state/local government agencies. [Source 1]

There is a critical unresolved issue: whether BIPA applies to biometric data that cannot identify a person. Some courts (e.g., Colombo v. YouTube, Gunderson v. Amazon) have allowed BIPA claims even where the defendant cannot identify the plaintiff from the data collected. Other courts (e.g., Daichendt v. CVS, Zellmer v. Meta) have held that BIPA requires the data to be capable of identifying a person. [Source 4]

**Section 15 — Retention, Collection, Disclosure, Destruction:** Private entities must:
- (a) Develop a public written policy establishing retention schedules and destruction guidelines. Data must be destroyed when the initial purpose has been satisfied or within 3 years of the individual's last interaction with the private entity, whichever occurs first.
- (b) Obtain informed written consent (including electronic signatures as of the 2024 amendment) before collecting biometric data.
- (c) Cannot sell, lease, trade, or otherwise profit from a person's or a customer's biometric identifier or biometric information.
- (d) Cannot disclose biometric data without consent, except for financial transactions, legal requirements, or court orders.
- (e) Must store and protect biometric data using reasonable industry standards (a "reasonable standard of care"). [Source 1, Source 25]

**Section 20 — Right of Action:** Any aggrieved person may sue in state circuit court or as a supplemental claim in federal district court. Penalties: $1,000 liquidated damages or actual damages (whichever is greater) for negligent violations; $5,000 liquidated damages or actual damages (whichever is greater) for intentional or reckless violations. Prevailing parties may also recover attorneys' fees, costs, and injunctive relief. The section also limits multiple recoveries for repeated violations involving the same biometric identifier and same person. [Source 1]

**Section 25 — Construction:** The Act does not apply to financial institutions subject to the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, does not conflict with HIPAA, and does not apply to contractors/subcontractors of state/local government agencies. [Source 1]

---

**PART 2: CONSENT MECHANISMS**

**Written Release Requirement:** BIPA requires that before collecting biometric data, a private entity must first: (1) inform the subject in writing that biometric data is being collected or stored; (2) inform the subject in writing of the specific purpose and length of term for which the biometric data is being collected, stored, and used; and (3) receive a written release from the subject. [Source 1, Source 23, Source 25]

**Electronic Signatures:** The 2024 amendment (SB 2979) updated the definition of "written release" to include "electronic signature," defined as "an electronic sound, symbol, or process attached to or logically associated with a record and executed or adopted by a person with the intent to sign the record." This confirms that checkboxes or other electronic confirmations are sufficient. [Source 12, Source 25, Source 28]

**Notice-and-Consent:** The core requirement is informed, written consent obtained BEFORE the first scan. This is described as "the single most common and costly mistake employers make, and it is the primary driver of BIPA class-action lawsuits." [Source 23]

**Opt-In vs. Opt-Out:** BIPA operates on an opt-in consent model. The statute requires affirmative written consent before collection. There is no opt-out mechanism; silence or inaction does not constitute consent. [Source 1, Source 23]

**In the Employment Context:** The statute defines "written release" to include "a release executed by an employee as a condition of employment," indicating the legislative intent for the Act to apply in the employment context. [Source 16]

---

**PART 3: PENALTY STRUCTURE**

**Statutory Damages (Section 20):**
- Negligent violations: $1,000 per violation, or actual damages (whichever is greater)
- Intentional or reckless violations: $5,000 per violation, or actual damages (whichever is greater)
- Additionally, prevailing parties may recover attorneys' fees, costs, and injunctive relief. [Source 1, Source 3]

**Discretionary Nature of Damages:** In Cothron v. White Castle System, Inc. (2023 IL 128004), the Illinois Supreme Court noted that damages under BIPA are discretionary, not mandatory, because Section 20 uses the word "may" rather than "shall." The court stated there is "no language in the Act suggesting legislative intent to authorize a damages award that would result in the financial destruction of a business." [Source 15, Source 16, Source 17]

**The 2024 Amendment and Per-Scan Damages:**

Prior to the 2024 amendment, under the Illinois Supreme Court's ruling in Cothron v. White Castle System, Inc. (2023 IL 128004), a separate claim accrued under BIPA each time a private entity scanned or transmitted an individual's biometric identifier or information. This created the potential for "annihilative liability" — White Castle estimated that class-wide damages could exceed $17 billion for 9,500 employees. [Source 2, Source 8, Source 17, Source 25]

The 2024 amendment (SB 2979 / P.A. 103-0769, effective August 2, 2024) clarified that when the same biometric identifier or biometric information of one individual is repeatedly collected or disclosed by the same defendant using the same method, those actions constitute a single violation for purposes of calculating statutory damages. The amendment provides that a private entity that collects biometric information "in more than one instance … from the same person using the same method of collection" has committed "a single violation" for which "the aggrieved person is entitled to, at most, one recovery under this Section." [Source 2, Source 7, Source 8, Source 10]

**The 2026 Seventh Circuit Ruling — Clay v. Union Pacific Railroad Co.:**

On April 1, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit issued a landmark ruling in Clay v. Union Pacific Railroad Co. (No. 25-2185, 7th Cir., Apr. 1, 2026), holding that the 2024 amendment to BIPA's damages provision (Section 20) applies retroactively to cases pending at the time of enactment (August 2, 2024). The court reasoned that the amendment affects remedies only, making it a procedural/remedial change (rather than a substantive change to BIPA's liability standards). The court noted that "Illinois courts have long treated remedial changes—including changes to statutory damages provisions—as procedural." [Source 2, Source 6, Source 7, Source 8, Source 9, Source 10, Source 11, Source 13, Source 27, Source 29, Source 30]

The court rejected plaintiffs' arguments that the amendment extinguished vested rights, noting that "Illinois plaintiffs have no vested right to a particular remedy" and that BIPA's statutory damages are discretionary. The court also rejected due process arguments, stating that "the amendment to Section 20 of BIPA raises no constitutional concerns" as "damages under BIPA are likely discretionary" and "this amendment decreases, rather than increases, the monetary penalties BIPA imposes on private entities." [Source 8, Source 13, Source 27]

The court identified two textual features demonstrating the amendment is a remedial provision: "the legislature located it in Section 20, not Section 15" and "the plain language of the amendment focuses on remedies." [Source 7, Source 10]

The financial stakes were substantial — one of the plaintiffs alleged that his fingerprint scans had been collected 1,500 times such that he alone was entitled to $7.5 million; the putative class action put billions in controversy. [Source 6, Source 9, Source 29]

The ruling addresses two certified questions from three consolidated district court cases (Gregg v. Central Transport LLC, No. 24-cv-00108 and Willis v. Universal Intermodal Services, Inc., No. 24-cv-00430): whether the amendment is a clarification applying to all pending cases, and whether it is retroactive. The Seventh Circuit held in favor of defendants on both questions. [Source 6, Source 29]

The decision may also require district courts to reassess federal subject-matter jurisdiction, as per-scan damages were previously used to satisfy the amount-in-controversy requirement. The ruling could result in dismissal or remand of several BIPA cases to state court for lack of jurisdiction. [Source 6, Source 29]

**Statute of Limitations:** In Tims v. Black Horse Carriers, Inc. (2023 IL 127801), the Illinois Supreme Court held that the five-year limitations period contained in section 13-205 of the Illinois Code of Civil Procedure governs claims under BIPA. [Source 5, Source 14, Source 22]

---

**PART 4: PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION**

**Who Can Sue:** "Any person aggrieved by a violation of this Act shall have a right of action in a State circuit court or as a supplemental claim in federal district court against an offending party." (Section 20(a)). [Source 1]

**Standing Requirements — Rosenbach v. Six Flags (2019 IL 123186):** In Rosenbach v. Six Flags Entertainment Corp. (2019 IL 123186), the Illinois Supreme Court held that a person need not sustain actual damages beyond a violation of their rights under BIPA in order to bring an action. The mere violation of the Act was sufficient to collect damages. The court ruled that users do not need to prove an injury (such as identity fraud or physical harm) in order to sue. [Source 3, Source 5, Source 22, Source 27]

This ruling led to a 1,400% increase in BIPA lawsuit filings, from 9 cases in 2018 to 134 in 2019, and 209 in 2020. Through September 2021, over 900 BIPA cases had been filed. [Source 19, Source 21, Source 27]

**PAGA-Style Claims:** BIPA does not contain a Private Attorneys General Act (PAGA)-style provision. There is no mechanism for private citizens to bring enforcement actions on behalf of the state. The private right of action is for individual or class-action claims only. [Source 1, Source 21]

**Class Action Dynamics:** 88% of BIPA lawsuits are employer-employee disputes from biometric timekeeping. 40% are filed against Illinois-based companies. In 8 consumer-oriented BIPA settlements, plaintiffs' lawyers received an average of $11.5 million per firm per case, while individuals received an average of $506 per case. [Source 19, Source 21]

**BIPA lacks procedural protections** such as notice and cure periods, safe harbors, damage caps, and exclusive AG enforcement — all recommended protections that other states have implemented. [Source 21]

---

**PART 5: TECHNOLOGY RESTRICTIONS**

**Definition of Biometric Identifiers:** "Biometric identifier means a retina or iris scan, fingerprint, voiceprint, or scan of hand or face geometry." (Section 10) [Source 1]

**What Is Excluded:** Writing samples, photographs, X-rays, medical images, and certain health information. [Source 1]

**Data Retention and Destruction Requirements:** A private entity in possession of biometric identifiers or biometric information must develop a written policy, made available to the public, establishing a retention schedule and guidelines for permanently destroying biometric identifiers and biometric information when the initial purpose for collecting or obtaining such identifiers or information has been satisfied or within 3 years of the individual's last interaction with the private entity, whichever occurs first. (Section 15(a)) [Source 1, Source 23]

**Prohibition on Selling Biometric Data:** "No private entity in possession of a biometric identifier or biometric information may sell, lease, trade, or otherwise profit from a person's or a customer's biometric identifier or biometric information." (Section 15(c)) [Source 1]

**Security Obligations:** Private entities must store and protect biometric data using reasonable industry standards. [Source 1, Source 3]

---

**PART 6: MAJOR ENFORCEMENT CASES**

**A. Rosenbach v. Six Flags Entertainment Corp. (2019 IL 123186)**

The Illinois Supreme Court ruled that a person need not have sustained actual damage beyond a violation of his or her rights under the Act in order to bring an action under it. This established that plaintiffs have standing based on mere procedural violations of BIPA, without any showing of actual injury. [Source 3, Source 5, Source 22]

**B. Cothron v. White Castle System, Inc. (2023 IL 128004)**

The Illinois Supreme Court, in a 4-3 decision, held that a separate claim accrues under the Act each time a private entity scans or transmits an individual's biometric identifier or information in violation of Section 15(b) or 15(d). The certified question from the Seventh Circuit was: "Do section 15(b) and 15(d) claims accrue each time a private entity scans a person's biometric identifier and each time a private entity transmits such a scan to a third party, respectively, or only upon the first scan and first transmission?" [Source 5, Source 15, Source 16, Source 17, Source 18]

The case involves Latrina Cothron, a White Castle employee since 2004, who filed a class action alleging that White Castle violated BIPA sections 15(b) and 15(d) by requiring employees to scan fingerprints to access pay stubs and computers without obtaining consent until 2018, a decade after the Act became effective in 2008. [Source 17]

**Key Reasoning from the Majority (Justice Rochford):**
- The plain language of Section 15(b) prohibits collecting, capturing, or obtaining biometric data without prior informed consent. The court found that "collect" and "capture" are not things that happen only once; each authentication scan constitutes a collection or capture because the system must capture the fingerprint each time for comparison.
- The "unless it first" phrase in Section 15(b) modifies the entity's obligation to obtain consent, not the triggering actions.
- Section 15(d) applies to every transmission to a third party. The terms "disclose" and "disseminate" are broad enough to include repeated transmissions to the same party.
- The court rejected White Castle's argument that injury occurs only upon initial loss of control, noting that Rosenbach established that the statutory violation itself is the injury.
- On the concern about potentially astronomical damages (White Castle estimated class-wide damages could exceed $17 billion for 9,500 employees), the court acknowledged the potential for significant awards but noted that damages are discretionary, not mandatory, under the Act, and suggested the legislature review these policy concerns. [Source 15, Source 17]

**Dissent (Justice Overstreet, joined by Chief Justice Theis and Justice Holder White):**
The dissent argued that the majority's interpretation "cannot be reconciled with the plain language of the statute," would lead to unintended consequences, and could "easily lead to annihilative liability for business." The dissent reasoned that the injury occurs only once—when biometric information is first obtained—as there is only "one loss of control or privacy." The dissent noted that in over 1,700 BIPA lawsuits since 2019, no plaintiff alleged a data breach or identity theft. Justice Overstreet argued that the majority's holding "subverted the intent of the Illinois General Assembly, threatens the survival of businesses in Illinois, and consequently raises significant constitutional due process concerns." The dissent noted that plaintiff Cothron alone could be entitled to over $7 million in damages for a single employee, despite no data breach or identity theft being alleged. [Source 14, Source 15, Source 16, Source 17]

The Illinois Supreme Court denied White Castle's petition for rehearing on July 18, 2023. [Source 14]

**Subsequent Legislative Fix:** The Illinois General Assembly responded with SB 2979, signed on August 2, 2024, which clarified that repeated collection of the same biometric identifier from the same person using the same method is a single violation allowing single recovery. [Source 12, Source 25, Source 28]

**C. Rogers v. BNSF Railway Co. (No. 1:19-cv-03083, N.D. Ill.)**

**Background:** This was the first BIPA case to go to trial in Illinois. On October 12, 2022, an Illinois jury ruled that BNSF Railway violated BIPA by scanning the fingerprints of 45,600 truck drivers without their written, informed consent when entering BNSF rail yards. The case involved BNSF's Auto-Gate System (AGS) at four Illinois railyards. BNSF contracted with Remprex (and previously Nascent) to install and manage the AGS. Remprex employees collected drivers' fingerprints (right thumb, left thumb, left index finger) without obtaining written consent or informing drivers of the specific purpose or retention period. [Source 5, Source 6, Source 7, Source 8, Source 9]

**Verdict:** The jury found that BNSF recklessly or intentionally committed 45,600 BIPA violations (one violation per class member), and the court entered a $228 million judgment (45,600 × $5,000 per violation). Lead plaintiff Richard Rogers said at a press conference after the verdict: "I'm really happy with the verdict today… all I ever wanted was justice for the over 45,000 truck drivers and myself." [Source 5, Source 6, Source 7, Source 8, Source 9]

**Vacatur and New Trial Order:** On June 30, 2023, U.S. District Judge Matthew Kennelly vacated the $228 million damages award and ordered a new trial limited to the question of damages. The court relied on the Illinois Supreme Court's decision in Cothron v. White Castle System, Inc., which noted that BIPA Section 20 uses the word "may" (discretionary) rather than "shall" (mandatory), meaning damages are discretionary, not mandatory. The court concluded that the amount of damages under BIPA Section 20 is discretionary and should be decided by the jury. [Source 7, Source 8, Source 9, Source 16]

**Settlement:** BNSF and the class ultimately reached a $75,000,000 settlement. The settlement website is bnsfbipaclassaction.com. The case is 2019-CH-04393. The court granted final approval on June 18, 2024, and payments were expected to mail on February 26, 2025. [Source 10]

Facebook settled a BIPA class action lawsuit for $650 million in 2020 (originally $550 million in January 2020, increased to $650 million in July 2020) over its "Tag Suggestion" facial recognition feature. The case was filed in 2015, alleging that Facebook violated BIPA by using facial recognition technology to extract and store biometric identifiers from up to six million Illinois users without their written consent. Approximately 1.6 million class members were eligible. [Source 28, Source 29]

Facebook also agreed to turn off its facial recognition feature for most class members and delete existing face templates unless users opted back in. Facebook discontinued its facial recognition feature entirely in November 2021, deleting templates of over 1 billion users. [Source 27, Source 29]

**E. McDonald v. Symphony Bronzeville Park, LLC (2022 IL 126511)**

On February 3, 2022, the Illinois Supreme Court unanimously held that the Workers' Compensation Act's exclusivity provisions do not bar a claim for statutory damages under BIPA when an employer is alleged to have violated an employee's statutory privacy rights. Marquita McDonald filed a putative class action against her former employer, Bronzeville, alleging that the company collected, used, and stored employees' fingerprints in a biometric timekeeping system without providing required disclosures or obtaining written releases. [Source 5, Source 16, Source 22]

The court held that the key question is whether the injury "categorically fits within the purview of the Compensation Act." The court concluded that BIPA violations — which involve the loss of the ability to maintain privacy rights and the right to withhold consent — are fundamentally different in nature from the physical and psychological workplace injuries compensable under the Compensation Act. The court noted that the BIPA postdates the Compensation Act and specifically contemplates its application in the employment context by defining "written release" to include "a release executed by an employee as a condition of employment." [Source 16]

**M. Svoboda v. Amazon.com Inc. (No. 25-1361, 7th Cir., Dec. 17, 2025)**

The Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed certification of a BIPA class action against Amazon. The lawsuit alleges Amazon's "virtual try-on" (VTO) technology, which uses augmented reality to overlay makeup and eyewear products on user images, violated BIPA by collecting, capturing, and storing facial geometry data of Illinois residents without proper consent. The district court had certified a class of individuals who used the VTO feature on Amazon's mobile website or app while in Illinois on or after September 7, 2016. The Seventh Circuit affirmed, holding that the same conduct—Amazon's alleged use of the VTO application—unites the BIPA claims, and that common issues regarding the software's functionality, Amazon's use of biometric data, and whether that use violated BIPA could be resolved "in one stroke." The class contains over 100,000 individuals. [Source 14]

Plaintiffs also claim Amazon uses the data for two purposes beyond tracking: improving JWO software and selling customer biometric data to other retailers, violating Section 15(c) of BIPA (which prohibits selling, leasing, trading, or profiting from biometric identifiers).
